FIELDING moved that the House go into Committee of Supply.

After committing the murder Private Moir obtained two revolvers and a rifle and a large quantity of ammunition and he disappeared from the barracks and has not been heard of since. The police of London have done their best to discover and apprehend the man, but he has got away into the country and the county constables are somewhat indifferent about attempting to arrest a man who is heavily armed in the manner in which this man is, aud I do not think that they have given the matter the attention that they should have. I think that if some moderate reward were offered for the capture of this man he would very likely be obtained. The gentleman whom he murdered was not a member of his corps at all. He was a colour-sergeant named Lloyd belonging to the 20th battalion of Stratford and he was only there taking a course of instruction in order to pass an examination which would qualify him to occupy a position in his regiment-a young man of twenty-two years. It is a very serious case and I think that something should be done by the government in the way of offering a moderate reward for his capture.
What kind of a rifle has he to defend himself with?.
That I do not know.

Before you leave the chair, Mr. Speaker, I would like to refer briefly to a matter which I mentioned a moment ago-the inquiry to be conducted by Mr. Justice Cassels and the manner In which that inquiry is to be carried out. We all realize that the inquiry is a very restricted one inasmuch as it relates to a portion of the administration and to only one of the departments involved in the

report of the Civil Service Commission. It touches only a single paragraph of the report of the commissioners in respect to that department. I have already pointed out to the House that it would have seemed a natural thing to have endeavoured, in the first place, to obtain from the commissioners who had made that report the information which is sought by the inquiry before Air. Justice Cassels. The commissioners who have made a somewhat exhaustive inquiry, although they say it is incomplete even in the case of the Department of Alarine and Fisheries, would seem to be the best men from whom an explanation of the language contained in the paragraph referred to might be sought. As far as the House is aware the government have not sought from these commissioners any explanation of their language, nor have the government invoked the aid of these commissioners for the purpose of obtaining the information which naturally they might be expected to supply. The government have not admitted at ail the expediency of sending back the report to the same commissioners for the purpose of reporting at greater length upon a subject to which the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Air. Brodeur) called attention on the day the report was presented. The government have not even seen fit to propose an inquiry under the first part of the statutes relating to public Inquiries. They have proposed a very limited inquiry into the second part of the statute which relates to such subjects. Since the inquiry has been ordered it is proposed that iMr. G. H. Watson, of Toronto, and Air. Perron, of Alontreal, two members of the bar of their respective provinces, shall be assigned for the purpose of assisting Air. Justice Cassels in the very limited inquirv which he is to carry out. I asked the'government whether or not the commissioners, whose report is, to a certain extent at least, under review^ in these proceedings, were to have any status before that commission, whether they were to be represented by counsel or whether their aid was to be invoked in the matter. Up to the present time no information has been vouchsafed in reply to that question. My hon. friend from Fast Hastings (Mr. Northrnp) inquired of the government whether or not the people of Canada wore to be represented by counsel. The right hon. Prime Alin-ister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), in reply to that question, stated that the matter would be taken into consideration. Up to the present time we have no reply from the government on that point.
It seems quite clear from this reply of the Prime Alinister that lie very properly regards the gentlemen who have been appointed as not representing the people of Canada, and the situation seems to be very much like this : The Department of Alarine and Fisheries is on trial in respect to ' Mr R. L. BORDEN
its administration of public affairs within the jurisdiction of that department ; the government on well known constitutional principles is also on trial because its fate is to a greater or lesser extent involved in the result of the investigation, and two gentlemen both of whom are very prominent Liberals have been appointed to assist Air. Justice Cassels in that investigation. Now, if I remember rightly, in 1891 when an investigation was carried on in respect of the Department of Public Works the government of Canada employed Air. B. B. Osier, who was affiliated with the Liberal party and not with the Conservative party, as one of the counsel to investigate that matter and to probe it to the bottom.
And Air. Geoffrion.

My hon. friend (Air. Bergeron) reminds me of what I was not aware that Air. Geoffrion, of Alontreal, who was also prominently associated with the Liberal party and who afterwards became a member of this government, was also appointed a counsel on that occasion. There is another somewhat remarkable circumstance in connection with this matter and it is this : We have had from the Alinister of Alarine and Fisheries on more than one occasion, the suggestion, or the excuse or the apology put forward that certain matters which had received criticism in connection with the administration of his department wrere matters for which he was not individually or personally responsible according to his view, because they had been initiated or consummated as the case may be under the administration of his immediate predecessor. And it appears that one of the gentlemen who has been appointed as counsel in this connection to assist Air. Justice Cassels was for many years a partner in the practice of the law with the immediate predecessor of the Alinister of Alarine and Fisheries. One can hardly appreciate or understand the reasons which have impelled the government to make selections of that character. One would suppose that if the aid of the first commissioners, Messrs. Courtney, Fyshe and Bazin was invoked they at least would have been called upon to make a statement before Air. Justice Cassels, and that counsel w'ould have been supplied to be nominated by these commissioners to whom they could have iven the information and whom they could have instructed as to the matters which they had reported on. One would suppose further, that if that very reasonable course were not adopted the government would at least have endeavoured to appoint men who had not been very actively associated with the Liberal party, who were not very closely in touch with the organization of the Liberal party ; in'short they would not have selected two men, one of whom Air. Watson was I understand not very long ago chairman of the Liberal organization for the

province of Ontario, and the other of whom, Mr. Perron was during the lifetime of the predecessor of the present Minister of Marine and Fisheries the partner of that gentleman in the practice of the law. Under these circumstances it is no more than right to bring the matter to the attention of the government and ask whether or not these commissioners are to be represented by counsel, whether or not the people of Canada are to be represented by cotinsel; and why it is that so extraordinary a choice of gentlemen to assist Mr. Justice Cassels has been made.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. P. BRODEUR (Minister of Marine and Fisheries).
speechtext: I may say at once that so far as the government is concerned nothing will be done to prevent this investigation being as thorough and as extended as possible. As head of that department I have every interest to see that the investigation shall be as complete as it can be. In the very brief interview I had with Judge Cassels the other day I told him that my aim was that officers of the department who had been derelict in their duty should not be spared, and that the cloud on those officers who were not guilty should be removed as speedily as possible. I may say-perhaps my hon. friend will not believe me-but the fact is that I am thoroughly in earnest about this investigation. I want to see the investigation made in such a way that no blame shall be attached to the government or to myself as head of the department as to its precedure. I want to see this investigation conducted in such a way that the people of Canada may be satisfied that the intention of the government and of the department is to make the investigation absolutely right in all respects. I repeat it -I am perhaps more in earnest than he is in wishing that this investigation shall be as thorough as possible. Now, the hon. gentleman finds fault that the investigation is to be held under the second part of chapter 104, but I think there was no discretion for us in the matter. The first part of the statute deals with investigations as to certain public affairs generally, such as the investigation held by the Civil Service Commission, but when we came to a departmental inquiry the statute says it is to be made under the second part of that statute. Whether the investigation is held under the first part or under the second part it can be conducted in absolutely the same way ; it can be as thorough in one case as in the other. It appears to be plain that when the investigation is into a matter of general public interest it comes under the first part of the statute and when it is a departmental investigation it is brought under the second part.
That would imply there is no public interest in this investigation.

Oh, no. The statute determines the class of investigation that shall
be held under each part. An inquiry affecting our commerce, or our transportation, or as to combines, would be under the first part of the statute, but a departmental investigation is to be made under the second part of the statute, and after all it really does not make very much difference.

I understand the minister to say that if it related to a matter which concerned the public it should be made under the first part of the statute, and if it were a matter that only concerned the department it was to be made under the second part of the statute. Therefore it occurred to me that if it were made under the second part it implied that the public had no interest in it.

There is no doubt the public is; interested, but I am not the author of tlie law, and the statute makes this distinction, and under the advice of the Minister of Justice this is the part of the statute under which the investigation should be held. The investigation will however be held just in the same way no matter which it comes under; witnesses will be examined under oath and the procedure will be the same. My hon. friend says no effort has been made to try to ascertain the opinion of the commission. Well, I suppose that would be a matter for the commissioners themselves to dispose of. It is not for us to suggest to the judge the way in which he should proceed. I want to leave him absolutely free to act as he Ikes in this investigation. I would not wish to make any suggestion to him which might be interpreted as restricting him in the exercise of his powers. I repeat that we want this investigation to be thorough ; and if I were to make any suggestion to the judge as to the way in which he should conduct the investigation, I might be reproached by the House with interfering with something that I should not interfere with. The commission gives to the judge the right to investigate this matter, and he is absolutely free, so far as the government or the department are concerned, to act in the way he likes ; and that is the position I will take all through this investigation. My hon. friend says that in several instances I have tried to shield myself behind my predecessor. I can assure my hon. friend that there is no intention of that kind on my part. I have never so far done anything, and never will do anything, to shield myself from any responsibility which attaches to me as Minister of Marine and Fisheries. I am manly enough to act as a man should act in such circumstances, and the responsibility I incur for the acts of my predecessor, I will never try to shield myself from that responsibility by going behind a corpse or a coffin. There are perhaps men in this House or outside of it who cannot understand a man taking that position. It has been stated that one of the

persons selected as a counsel in this investigation has been for some time a partner of my predecessor in office. It is true, before itfr. Prefontaine was a minister, when he was first elected mayor of Montreal, he dissolved partnership with Mr. Perron, and that fact was publicly announced. Do I understand that my hon. friend wants now to attack the character of Mr. Prefontaine? I think it was the hon. member for Grenville (Mr. J. D. Reid) who said a short time ago that Mr. Prefontaine was an honest man and that there was nothing against him. Do I understand that the hon. member for Grenville is now standiug by his words ?
I said that if you or any other man on that side of the House was afraid to stand up and defend him, I was prepared to do it. But every one on that side was afraid to do it.

I understand that my hon. friend from Grenville said that there was nothing against Mr. Prefontaine ? If that is the case, why does the hon. leader of the opposition say that we want to prevent the truth coming out so far as Mr. Prefontaine is concerned ? No ; there is nothing that the government want to conceal in this matter. We want the truth and the whole truth to come out, and perhaps we shall find some truth that will surprise somebody.

Mr. Speaker, if we were looking for a party success I believe we should refrain from criticising the position taken by the government, because to my mind they have put themselves in the worst possible position. What are the facts? The government appointed a commission composed of three men in whom they must have had confidence-honest, honourable men. The chairman of that commission was in the Finance Department for over thirty years, enjoying the respect and esteem of both sides of this House ; Mr. Fyshe, of Montreal, well known in commercial circles, and Mr. Bazin, of Quebec. That commission went to work and made a report. That report was entirely against the present administration. With regard to two departments which they investigated, the Marine and Fisheries and the Militia, their report could not have been more severe. They declared that they had not time to investigate the other departments, but from what they heard, if they had had time to investigate them, they would probably have had the same report to make with regard to them all. That is the report. What does the government do ? The government, to place themselves in a good position before the public, should have acted on that report. The man on the street, who is not prejudiced, would have expected the government to act on that report immediately. The man on the street would have expect-Mr. BRODEUR.
ed the government to say to the commission :	We want you to continue and go
through all the departments ; we want to show the public that we are in earnest, and that if there is anything wrong in any of the departments, we want to put an end to it. But the government of Canada did not do that. They seemed to be disappointed with the report of the commission ; they seemed to think the commission should not have made a report of that kind, and they appointed another commission to investigate the first commission ; that is what it means. It means that the government are under the impression that a new commission will attenuate the report of the first commission. My hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries has said so. He says, we want the employees who are guilty punished and the employees who are not guilty vindicated. That could all be done by the report of the present commission. We do not want another commission for that purpose.
There are no names given in the report of the present commission.
My hon. friend knows very well what it means, however. I am sure he knows.
What does it mean ?

I am not appointed as a new commission to make a report. Personally I think the government could not be in a worse position than they are. I think this new commission is entirely useless. We are told that Judge Oassels is an honourable man. I believe that, but what I am surprised at, and I do not see any reason for it, is the idea of appointing lawyers. My hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries says that it was at the suggestion of the judge that these lawyers were appointed. Of course, I take for granted that what he says is true ; but I am astonished that Judge Cassels should have asked for anything of the kind. And who are the lawyers appointed ? My hon. leader has said that when an investigation took place into the Department of Public Works under a Conservative administration, lawyers were appointed at the demand of the Liberal party, then in opposition, to go through the books and other documents in the Public Works offices at that time. The Conservative administration, though having a very large majority, granted that demand. And who were the lawyers appointed ? The government might have appointed some Conservative lawyers ; but instead of that, they appointed two Liberal lawyers at the suggestion of the then opposition. How different that is from the present case. I am told that one of the gentlemen appointed to-day. Mr. Watson, is or lias been at the head of the Liberal or-

ganization in the province of Ontario. He may again be president, a strong party man, a strong friend of the present administration. The other one, Mr. Perron, is as strong a partisan as could be found in the whole Dominion of Canada; he has been engaged in nearly every contested election trial that has taken place in Montreal, he is looked upon as the staunchest friend of hon. gentlemen opposite. All his life since he became a lawyer he has been a partner of Mr. Pr6-fontaine. My hon. friend said that Mr. Prefontaine had resigned from that firm. We all know what that means ; Mr. Pr6-fontaiue was a member of the firm until he died. His name did not appear, but he was a member of the firm of Archer, Perron & Taschereau. And Mr. Perron is called in as a lawyer in this investigation. I would not say a word against his personality, but we all know how far a man can go for party purposes, and I would say, if it was not so serious, what a farce it would be to have a report from Mr. Cassels assisted by Mr. Perron and Mr. Watson against the report of a commission appointed by this government less than a year ago. The government could not be in a worse position. Tile appointment of Mr. Perron may satisfy the Liberals of Montreal, staunch Liberals who expect something from the government -because those are the only ones to-day who stand by them-but the independent elector, the man who is looking for an honest report, will certainly blame the administration and will have no confidence in the report that Judge Cassels will make. This is another way of spending money, this is another part of the combine. Judge Cassels, I understand, will not be paid any extra fee, he is paid as judge of the -Exchequer Court about $8,000 a year. But how will tli* two lawyers be paid? I believe they will be paid $100 a day each. I do not believe that Mr. Perron would work for less than $100 a day, and he would be very foolish to do so, because if he asks that amount he will get it. How long will the inquiry last? I repeat that the man on the street, the public, will be disgusted with the lavish way in which this government is spending the public money. I am sorry for the good of Canada that the commission which made the first report has not been called upon to go through every department in Ottawa. The government should be interested in having such an investigation. When I look at the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance I have no doubt they are interested in seeing whether proper investigation is made into every department at Ottawa. We will not have such an investigation, as that branch of the inquiry is finished; this will be an investigation of the investigation. It will be something done to try and whitewash what has been said in condemnation of the two departments in which the investigation has been going on.

The hon. gentleman sees that the commissioners in their report say there is a lack of conscience on the part of some officers of the department. At the same time no names are mentioned, no persons are singled out. Does he think I should continue to administer the department with the same staff without taking the proper steps to investigate and find out who are the guilty parties?
I want to say that my hon. friend could have done all that if he wanted to, without having a new commission.
How would you do it?

I am not going to tell my hon. friend and the House. I will tell my hon. friend privately, it could be done in two hours. When the commission makes a report that in his department money is lavished, that it is the most extravagant department at Ottawa, that it is squandering money, that it has no conscience, that there is only one aim, to spend money, that no discount is obtained as in ordinary trade, it is clear as day to me. The money is not used for religious purposes, it has gone somewhere. Why the hon. member does not need to appoint another commission; in two hours he could find a remedy and could save the money of the country.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Minister of Finance).
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think the hon. gentleman who has just spoken, and the leader of the opposition also, have an entirely erroneous impression of the nature of the inquiry on which Judge Cassels is about to enter. They have assumed that the inquiry of Mr. Justice Cassels is a review of the work of the commission whose report has already been presented to the House. Nothing could be more erroneous than that conception of Judge Cassels' duty.
What is it then?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Judge Cassels' duty is to inquire into certain matters as to which the commission seemed to have failed to prosecute their investigation to the end. The commissioners' report may be deemed to be divided into two parts. One part of it relates to the ordinary questions of the civil service, such as the conditions of admission, examinations, promotions, salaries, &e., questions of a broad and important class. In addition to that there is another branch and that probably is the branch which has received the most attention and consideration by the public, that is the accusation made in somewhat general terms, of not mismanagement, but much worse. It is practically stated in the report of two of the commissioners, Messrs. Fyshe and Bazin, that there has been corruption in the Department of Marine and Fisheries. The word is not used but my hon. friend says he knows what the report means.
So do you.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, I will be frank and say I do not know what it means. I know in a general way, but I certainly think, with all deference to the gentlemen composing the commission, for whom I hare the greatest respect, that on that particular point it is a fair criticism to say that the commission has said either too much or too little. If they wished to go into that branch of the question-and I do not say they should not have done so-as to whether or not the officials in the service were corrupt, then they were bound in justice to themselves, to the House, and the individuals concerned, to go further, and say in some detail who was corrupt and wherein the corruption lay. 'mat is the only criticism I offer on the report of the commission As to its general recommendations, I do not call them in question. We will have to deal with them later. My hon. friend says: Why not deal with them? Whether or not we will deal with them has to be considered. If we fail to deal with them at all, we shall be no worse than hon. gentlemen opposite who had a similar report in 1892, kept it for four years and did nothing.
It was not complete.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The report was most complete, and if my hon. friend does not want to take the trouble to read it, he may have seen in the Ottawa Conservative paper in the last week, three or four letters from a civil service official, calling attention to the fact that years ago, in 1892, four yems before the Conservative government left office, a report was made by a civil service commission dealing with practically the same classes of questions as are referred to in this report, the question of the political influence exercised in relation to patronage, the inequality of salaries, the purchase of supplies-all these questions were reported on by that commission, which included one of the gentlemen who sat on the recent commission. The hon. gentlemen opposite remained in power for four years from the date of that report without attempting any remedy whatever. So, if it should be the policy of this government, and I hope it will not, to pay no attention whatever to the report of the commission, if we should be simply content to receive it, pigeon-hoie it and forget it, we would be on even terms with my hon. friends opposite, because that was precisely their course with regard to the report of the commission of 1892 as will be explained later on if necessary.
The report of the commission of 1892 and the report of the last commission are not at all alike.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Let me mention some respects in which they are alike. They are aliice in the allegation that political patronage enters largely into appointments.
Mr FIELDING
Yes. That is not a crime.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is not a crime, but the commissioners said that was a great evil. They said that in 1892 and it is said -by the present commissioners. But while in 1892, that evil, so far as it is an evil, was pictured by that commission in their report just as it is pictured to-day, the Conservative government of that day pigeon-holed the report and took no notice of it.
And the same thing may happen in this case, so far as that point is concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If it should happen, then my hon. friend (Mr. Bergeron) will be in a position to assail us ; but the time has not come yet.	,

I say it is not a crime.
It is something that takes time and is very hard to do. . But when the commission said that stealing goes on. that robbery goes on, that corruption exists, it is a very different thing.	[DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But I want to come to some other things in the commission of 1892. That commission reported on the question of supplies. We had a debate here, not many days ago, on that question. Whatever evils there may be in regard to the patronage element in the purchase of supplies existed in 1892 ; it was reported on in 1892 ; it was fully exposed to the Conservative government of that day,-and they took no notice of it. In that respect, the report of 1892 and the report of the present day are substantially alike. My hon. friend says there is corruption, there is dishonesty-
' Lack of conscience.'

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, ' lack of conscience'. Now, my hon. friend says he knows what that means. I wish to be candid and to say that, as respects any officer of the Marine-and Fisheries Department, I do not know what it means. I know what it means generally ; I know what thieving, robbery means. But surely my hon. friend would not have this government, on the strength of that report-which, on that branch of the subject, I say is incomplete-lie would not have the Minister of Marine and Fisheries dismiss men now in the service on the ground of dishonesty. Would he have these men, some of them employed for many years in the public service, branded with the charge of dishonesty and dismissed ? Surely he would not. He may suggest that now, but if he had that sense of responsibility which men in public office ought to have, he would say that such a course would be utterly unfair and unjust.

Would the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fielding) allow me ? That is

what is going to happen it what the Minister of Marine and Fisheries says is carried out. He says that he wants a commission to find out and punish the men

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bergeron) says he knows who these men are.	-
It is clear, for instance, that they are not the officers of the Department of Finance. They are employees of this department which has been reported upon.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But the hon. gentleman will see that ' employees of the Marine and Fisheries Department' is a broad and general expression. The misfortune is that the commission,-unintentionally ; they are not lawyers, but good business men-have generalized in such a way as to leave the whole department under a ffloud as respects dishonesty.
Will the minister (Mr. Fielding) allow me a question ? Why did not the government refer this back to the commissioners to find out who these men are ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The commission, in the first place, had unlimited power. They had the right to report as they have done, of course. They were free to take their own course. They took all the time they wanted. And they reported to the best of their judgment. Unfortunately, they left this particular branch of the business in an unfinished state ; and it is the unfinished business as respects the reflections upon the integrity of the Department of Marine and Fisheries that Mr. Justice Cassels has been asked to inquire into. Not the integrity of tlie Minister of Marine and Fisheries ; that }s not called into question. Let there be no misunderstanding on that point. We know the doctrine of constitutional responsibility and we accept it. If an official of my department in Victoria, B.C., should betray his trust and steal the public money, there is a constitutional sense in which I should be responsible, and so should my right hon. friend the Prime Minister and all my colleagues. We know, I say, what constitutional responsibility is, and we are prepared to accept that without the slightest hesitation. But there is more than the mere question of constitutional responsibility in this matter. So far as the Minister of Marine and Fisheries is concerned, let it be stated clearly and beyond all question that there is not a a line in the report of the Civil Service Commission which, even in the most shadowy way, reflects upon the integrity, the honour or the independence of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Brodeur). It is not pretended that there is any responsibility upon the minister other than that constitutional responsibility which we are ready
to accept. But there is not only the constitutional responsibility which I have described, there is the individual responsibility for acts of dishonesty. Now the commission have given it to be understood that there have been acts of dishonesty on the part of officials of the Marine and Fisheries Department. It is not fair to leave these officials, many of them old employees in the public service, under that imputation. And so, with a view to prosecuting the inquiry further. this reference is made to Mr. Justice Cassel#. There can be no question as to the propriety of that course. While, in the case of questions of classification of officials, salaries of officials and matters of that character, the opinion of any good business man may be valuable, yet, when you come to make an inquiry that will affect a man's honour, his character, his repputation his standing in life, who so well qualified to couduct that investigation, as a judge of one of the higher courts? Surely, if we were to have a further inquiry into that branch of the question, it was eminently fitting that the inquiry should be conducted by a gentleman holding the high position of Judge Cassels.
With regard to the selection of the legal gentleman, I think there is an important difference between the situation in 1891 and the situation of to-day. In the proceedings in 1891. accusations were made against members of this House-accusations, I might almost say, against ministers, because they Involved ministers in the end. But that is not the situation to-day. There is no accusation here against any minister ; there is nothing alleged in the report of the Civil Service Commission which, even if proved to the last point, would call for the retirement of any hon. member of this House. There is no allegation of wrong as affecting any minister or member of this House. The allegation is of lack of conscience. in fact, of dishonesty, on the part of some of these officials. Now, it so happens that most of the officials of the Department of Marine and Fisheries, especially the older officials and those holding more responsible positions, were appointed in years gone by by the Conservative government. What would have been said if the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to-day, acting upon that vague and indefinite report-for, upon that branch of the subject, it is vague and indefinite-had proceeded to dismiss officials appointed years ago by the Conservative party, with no better grounds than the indefinite statements of that report ? What would have been said by gentlemen opposite ? They would have been the first to attack the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. They would have said : You had not any evidence ; you had only vague and general charges ; but you seized upon these and made them the excuse for dismissing old officials appointed by the

Conservative government. We were not prepared to give occasion for an accusation of that character. I trust that, no matter who might be the officials concerned, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries would not be willing to take that course. But, when ,we remembered that a charge of that kind would affect the chief officials, when we remembered that these were gentlemen who have occupied positions in the civil service for many years and who had received their appointments from the preceding government, I think that every consideration of right and fairness and justice would lead us to say that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries took the right course when he declared that he would not dismiss men on the strength of this report, but inasmuch as their honour, their conscience has been called in question, has declared that he will carry on a further inquiry on that particular branch of the subject-not reviewing the report of the commission, but taking up the case where the commission left it off -and. in the light of such a full and fair investigation as shall take place, then let justice be done.

The defence which has been put up by the two lion, gentlemen who have spoken has shot wide entirely of the mark, so far as it attempted to answer the very temperate observations which were made by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries thought that all he had to do to answer that was, in the first place, to make repeated and strong asseverations of his own honour and integrity and his complete desire to see the public service purged, and then he wound up with an ill-concealed threat that before he got through with the investigation we on this side of the House would find out something that we did not know before. The threat was a very plain one; he has used it so often that the moment the boil, gentleman frames his lips we know exactly what is coming. The threat concealed in part, but still open enough, is : We will have our vengeance out of you anyway, because we will punish some of the old officials belonging to the Marine Department. Now, that was not very dignified, not very satisfactory, nor was it politically a very astute defence for the hon. gentleman to make in reference to matters in his department. He has been very anxious indeed to separate himself absolutely from the department. His colleagues are equally anxious, because they know as well as he does that it is impossible constitutionally or practically to separate the head of the department from misdoings of the department itself. They are all very anxious to make it clear if they can to the public, if they cannot make it so to this House, that

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
More than a month has passed and the report, as incisive, full and particular as it is, lies there to this day without another move. They have spoken of the commission that they themselves appointed and in reference to its constituents they have given it the highest praise; yet the report declares that there is a department without a head and without a conscience. A month has passed and what has been done? Hon. gentlemen say, and this order in council says, to put it in plain English, that inasmuch as certain general accusations or inferences have been made in the report, that there has not been strict business honesty in carrying on the affairs of the department, we will have a commission which will examine really into what?-to And out whether anybody has taken bribes or has been guilty of personal dishonesty as regards the carrying out of the transactions of the department as employees of the same. That is all. Judge Cassels is not to touch upon the weightiest of all matters, the utter disorganization, inefficiency and lack of business method in the department. These gentlemen say: We want to find out the truth; we do not want these general accusations to lie against any members of our staff and consequently we will appoint Judge Cassels to look into it. But, before Judge Cassels is appointed and before he does a stroke of work the minister himself undertakes to do what they say they want a commission to do, and he has suspended, one, two, or three of his officers [DOT] and is conducting a departmental inquiry of his own. Why, what he wanted Judge Cassels appointed for was to do that very thing, and it seems to me that the hon. gentleman who presides over that department ought not for a single instance to have undertaken any Inquiry into these matters himself when they were relegated to the commissioner who was appointed for that purpose and who was appointed because of these very reasons and these only.
The hon. Minister of Justice was good enough to, say, in his speech in his own constituency, that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries was carrying on an investigation in his own department, that he was weeding out the Tory goats from the Liberal sheep, I suppose, and further it was asserted by the Minister of Justice, who had appointed a commission to find out something which he did not know, and which the government wanted to know, that the Tory goats should be well punished by dismissal for their wrong-doings in the matter of their departmental work. What a spectacle it is to have a government, which wants to know something and cannot make a decision until it finds it out and has Judge Cassels appointed to investigate; pronouncing judgment themselves as individual members of the cabinet! The Minister of Marine and Fisheries did so and the Minister of Justice, of all men in the world, did so in his speech in his own constituency the other Mr. FOSTER
night. That is British justice. That is one way of doing things, but it does not seem to me to be the best way. Ah, but the Minister of Marine and Fisheries was wonderfully anxious to find out just who had been doing these things. There had been different accusations, if you call them such, but which I would rather call inferences, by Messrs. Courtney, Fyshe and Bazin. What would be simpler than to say to these gentlemen: We want you to give us the facts from which you drew these inferences. These gentlemen are responsible men; they have the Prime Minister's and the government's own endorsement of their character and ability.
They went into it themselves, they investigated it, they made their report and the inferences or accusations are a part of that report. If the government wanted to know exactly who they were, what more simple than to ask these gentlemen to further amend the report by giving the special instances. That would have been an easy thing to do. Why, if the government wanted the information did they not take that short business cut and get the information that the commissioners have on their note books or within their minds, because it is they who made the report in which these accusations or inferences are brought out which are referred to Judge Cassels. What happens now ? The Minister of Marine and Fisheries says he is intensely desirous that the whole truth shall be brought out and what does he do ? He appoints a commission to investigate himself under the idea that he is not investigating himself but certain officials in his department. It is a commission appointed by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries himself as the order in council goes, differently worded from a general commission. And then the Minister of Marine and Fisheries who is the person responsible, who is the person implicated and the person whom the public will hold responsible ; he appoints his own counsel to carry on the prosecution in the case, absolutely appoints his own counsel. He is being tried, his efficiency or inefficiency is to be shown in this investigation. Talk as you like, if this gentleman who is at the head of the department has guided for two years a department with that sort of thing going on and has not found it out and has not reformed it and has not put it in good directive condition, the minister himself must have the responsibility. He is the man who is really on trial and yet he appoints a commissioner who is for all we know to carry on the investigation in camera, and then he appoints two red hot partisans in order to shield himself and his department. There cannot be any other inference Hon. gentlemen may say what they please. They may try to make themselves believe what they please but the country at large will not be satisfied with that kind of dealing. The country will say:

These gentlemen want to mitigate the force of a report which has struck them hard and they try to mitigate it by appointing an in camera investigation and then by putting their own hard and fast partisans on to carry out the investigation. But, you say, Judge Casseis will carry on the investigation. Yes, but these are the counsel through whom he is to carry it on. They are the men that are to advise what witnesses should be brought and what cases should be taken up. They are the men who are to steer the whole investigation. Judge Casseis, cannot do it, it is not his position, he is in tlie way of a judge, an inquiring judge of course. But the cases have to be brought and the witnesses have to be brought, and who shall lie shielded and who shall not be shielded, that is the part of Mr. Perron and of Mr. Watson and they are being paid their fees in order to do that part. Now, will the country stand for that sort of thing ? I ask my right hon. friend if he thinks the country will. If he is imagining such a vain tiling as that he will wake up some day and find he is mistaken in his imaginings. The least the government can do is to make the investigation openly. If they want some of their own partisans to defend themselves let them get them and pay the country's money for that if necessary; but let them put some one there who has at heart the State's interest and no other interest than the State's interest, as a prosecutor to bring [DOT]evidence and to bring up the cases. For instance, what is one of the glaring cases. It is with reference to your Commissioner of Lights. Now. Sir, we have been told by the Minister of Justice that these were Tory goats who had got the Minister of Marine and Fisheries into all this trouble. Was the Commissioner of Lights a Tory goat ? Will you take his appointment and his salary when these gentlemen came into power in 1896 ; will you take his specific appointments since and his increases of salary from time to time, and the responsibilities that have been put upon him ; will you put all this together and say that it was simply a Tory goat that was working all this time, and that it was the purpose of the minister to weed him out from the Liberal sheep in that department. This is a gentleman who was appointed by the minister, who was chosen by the minister, who was given almost absolute power by the minister, who went into the business of the buoys and fog signals as though, to look at the commissioner's report, he were the paid employee of these two great concerns interested chiefly in finding out how much he could buy from them and where he could find a place to store the goods before they were wanted for actual use. The minister cannot escape from the responsibility in that case. Was it a Tory goat who made the arrangement with Falconer, an arrangement which on the' face of it is so child-like and so unbusinesslike that you would think no 233
sane man, mature and grown up man would be guilty' of. None of these things were committed by these Tory goats. Now I ask the minister if he proposes to go into that transaction of his Commissioner of Lights, who, to the extent of $1,000,000 worth of new apparatus within two years patronized one single concern and caused the commission to say, as they went through the astounding history, that it looked as if that body had their _qwu servant at work in the department. Will the minister have Judge Casseis root that out from the bottom 1 Is that a portion of Judge Cassel's work ? Will Mr. Watson, King's Couucel, take it up and push it ? Will Mr. Perron go into that business ? Is that what is to be done, or, are these gentlemen simply in chamber to find out how little they can bring out, how much they cam shield the government and how far they can go to keep the grand old party from getting what is rightly its due ? They have been 12 years in power, they have had their chosen men in that department and at the end of that time it is pictured to the public as a department without a head, without direction, and without conscience. The people of this country want a full investigation, they' want it in the light of open day, they want it fair and not loaded, they want to see somebody who is not a paid and partisan friend of the minister, interested in bringing the evidence and in making there searches before Judge Casseis.

The Minister of Finance seemed to take comfort to himself that there was no imputation against the Minister of Marine and Fisheries in the report of the Royal Commission. I take distinct issue with the hon. gentleman upon this point. What I complain of particularly in regard to the reference to Judge Casseis is that it is an isolated charge takeu out of the body of the charges made by the commissioners, in which is included a charge and imputation against the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, as distinct a charge as could possibly be made. I want to call the attention of the House to the fact that in the report, both before and after the statement which is referred to Judge Casseis, there are statements equally as damaging as the statement which is referred to the judge. And when the minister says in the order in council :
The minister observes that some statements are made in that report which affect the honour and integrity of the officers of the Department of Marine and Fisheries.
He fails to grasp the significance and meaning of the Royal Commission because that report, as I read it, is not directed to the officers of the department alone but to the head of the department as well. Let us see whether this is correct or not. They say on page 33 :



Your commissioners have spent a large an.ount of time trying to get an insight into the general administration of the government business, as shown in the management cl this department. They found that to make any efficient inspection was a matter of enormous difficulty.
And they point out the reasons for that. They Indicate that they have not made an exhaustive inquiry; hut they leave it as a clear inference that, if the government desires to know the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth, they are quite prepared to go on and investigate further. I want to call your attention to the fact that they are speaking, not of goats or of sheep,* but of a department; and when they are speaking of a department, they are speaking of an hon. gentleman who is at the head of the department, and who said this afternoon that more than all he desired a complete and thorough and extensive investigation. On page 34 they say :
There are officers enough in the department, both inside and outside, to do all the work efficiently, if they were properly trained and organized; but there is no efficient organization.
Are they pointing at the subordinates or at the head? I understand that the head is responsible for the organization, and if the head is not able to perform the duties of the organization for which he is responsible, he should resign. They go on to say :
It is practiallv impossible to fix responsibility on anybody.
Does that responsibility rest upon these unfortunate subordinates whom the minister has suspended, whom he tries himself and makes guilty by his own act before a proper investigation is had? The report continues :
Tlie' deputy is supposed to shoulder responsibility for everything, as his signature shows; but that means that he speaks for ' the department ' and ' the department/ like the King, can do no wrong.
That we hardly believe.
Theoretically.

Theoretically only, of course. The commissioners go on to say:
There seems to be a huge redundancy of work, which proceeds in a lumbering haphazard way, giving rise to constant mun-dering and confusion.
Whose act is that? Is that the act of the deputy head? Is that the act of a chief clerk or of a second-class clerk, or is it the act of the responsible minister of the Crown, who is at the head of the Marine and Fisheries Department? I take it, that applies to the head of the department- that ' there seems to be a huge redundancy of work, which proceeds in a lumbering, haphazard way, giving rise to constant Mr. LENNOX.
blundering and confusion.' Does the minister want to leave that on record? Is he satisfied that his department should be so characterized? Then they say :
There is no sign visible of a single directing head or an intelligent purpose, unless it be that of spending as much money as possible.
Who is the head of that department ? Who should be the single directing head ? Who should be the man of intelligent purpose to control the expenditure of the department, and to see that extravagance and dishonesty and graft .do not prevail? Who but the minister, who says: Wait till we have an investigation, and we will show what will surprise some hon. gentlemen- meaning, with that cowardly threat, that Conservative members of his department will suffer. We have it so far pretty clear that these gentlemen are speaking, not of subordinates, but of the Department of Marine and Fisheries. Wha4 are they talking of? They are talking of paying two prices where we should only pay one; they are talking of paying dishonest prices when we should only pay honest prices; and does the minister want to escape on the plea that for two long years all this has been going on in his department and he has been absolutely ignorant of the fact that we have been paying for goods at these dishonest and extravagant prices ? These gentlemen go on to say :
Zeal for economy and good management, or pride in the work, is not visible.
What are they speaking of ? They are speaking, as the heading indicates, of the Department of Marine and Fisheries. No attack, says my hon. friend, upon the Minister of Marine and Fisheries; no imputation against him; and my hon. friend waxes eloquent on that point, and thinks he has settled the question. I want to say here and now that we have not all the people before the court in this inquiry before Judge Casseis ; that when it is referred to Judge Casseis to try the officals of this department, the record is not complete ; that if you are to have a fair trial, an honest trial, a thorough and efficient trial, which the minister says he desires, it would not be alone to find out whether certain officials of the department are guilty or not, but to find out where the minister stands in regard to this matter as well. They go on to say:
Perfunctory and mechanical discharge of duties is the rule, with apparently no perception of any need for improvement.
And I suppose that If there were any improvement inaugurated, it would naturally be by the head of the department. Then the report says :
The lack of organization and of organizing power in tlie deoartment has recently been very conspicuously and painfully illustrated

by the fact that the accountant's or book' keeping branch had apparently fallen into such confusion that expert accountants had to be called in to put things to rights and create some intelligible system. After months of work by these highly paid experts, the result has been at least greatly improved books as far as mechanical form is concerned, but probably little else; and this achievement has been accomplished at an almost fabulous expense.
Then we come to the paragraph which my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries has seen fit to refer to Judge Cassels; but, mark you, he did not see fit to refer the whole of it. He thought it desirable to leave out the first sentence, which shows the meaning of a great deal of what follows :
There is not only a lack of efficient organization and method in the department.
Then follows what my hon. friend refers to Judge Cassels ;
There would also seem to be a lack of conscience.
A lack of conscience where, when you take the whole clause? A lack of conscience in the department, and so in the hon. minister himself. I need not follow with what is set out in the order in council, as my hon. friend has had it printed; but I may point out that this does not. even as printed here, mean that the commissioners thought the officials were responsible, but means that they were of opinion that the minister was responsible; and to show that I will read what Is set out here. I will read just what is said following the words in reference to the department:
There would also seem to be a lack of conscience. In connection with the enormous expenditures which are deemed necessary, the word 'discount ' never appears. It is tacitly assumed there is no such thing; but the whole commercial world knows otherwise. If no one gets any benefit from trade with the government except the trader, then it must be clear that in these great purchases made for the government, without discount, its officers must be assisting the trader to get better prices from the government than he can get anywhere else; for everywhere else he has to give a discount.
Down to that point there is nothing to indicate that it is the officials who are charged with dishonesty ; it is a general charge of dishonesty in the administration of the department at the expense of the country. What follows shows clearly that the commissioners had it in their minds that the officials are doing this either in ignorance or upon an intimation that the government wants it done in this way.
In other words, some of the government officials are serving two masters and apparently succeeding with both-scripture notwithstanding-
Whom do the commissioners mean by two masters ? They mean serving the seller and the buyer. The buyer is the minister ; they are serving two masters, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries and at the same time the men who are selling to the department. Does anybody believe, with our experience of what has taken place in the last eleven or twelve years, that this thing is done for love or for any other purpose than to enable these men who sell to the government to have the means, if they see fit, to assist the government when a crisis comes and an election is coming on ? No other reasonable construction can be put upon this paragraph than that these officers have either acted ignorantly or are acting by connivance with the government in paying prices much too high. That is borne out more strongly still by the expression.
-and apparently succeeding with both.
If the commissioners had not in their minds that they were acting in concert with the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, why should they use that phrase that they were apparently succeeding with both, scripture notwithstanding ? The minister is endeavouring to narrow this inquiry and secure an unfair advantage because if he had wanted to have the thorough, broad and complete investigation he says, why should he select this paragraph out of what I have read and what follows and refer that merely to the judge. He is not giving Judge Cassels a proper chance to try this case at all. If we are to believe what the minister says as to his desire for a full investigation, would he not have made the investigation as broad as I have suggested ? The minister seemed to have a doubt as to whether we could believe him. He said : I do not know whether hon. gentlemen will believe me or not but my object is to have a full and thorough investigation. Let me say to him now that if he had been desirous of convincing the members of the opposition or, what is far more important, the people of Canada, of his bona fides and honesty in this matter, he would have secured that end by referring to Judge Cassels, not an isolated sentence but the whole matter of his department, or else referring it back to the commissioners who had cast the aspersions upon him and his department.
The Minister of Finance also says that this is not a review. It is not a review, it is a good deal more than that, it is an attack upon the Royal Commission and as it stands to-day it is an appeal. The very day that this report was placed upon the table of the House the minister made an attack. He did not conceal his motive, he was clear and distinct. His statements are on ' Hansard '. He stated what he thought of this report and amongst other things claimed that the commissioners had gone beyond their duties and beyond the scope of what was referred to them. I

care not whether they went beyond the scope of what was referred to them or not, they have found a certain amount of truth, they have laid it before the House and if the minister wanted to ascertain the names of the men referred to in the report it would have been an easy matter to consult the commissioners. But the minister made his attack and then he followed it up. And what is he doing now ? He is putting these commissioners upon trial. The language he uses in his own order of reference, in the order in council, makes that perfectly plain.
The minister observes that some statements are made in the report ivhich affect the honour and integrity of officers of the Department of Marine and Fisheries. On page 61 of the report the following paragraph appears.
Then he quotes the paragraph.
The minister further observes that it is assumed by that statement that commissions are received improperly, or enhanced prices paid through dishonesty on the part of officials of the Department of Militia and Defence.
I have already pointed out that it is not confined to the officials of the Marine and Fisheries Department. He says then, as the result of the whole matter :
The minister therefore recommends that he be authorized to appoint the Hon. Walter Cassels a commissioner under part 2 of chapter 104 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1906. to investigate and report upon the foregoing statements contained in the said report.
His department is on trial but he selects his own judge. No one will argue for one moment that in view of the language used by the hon. gentleman himself, this is not a clear and distinct appeal and an endeavour to reverse the statement of the commissioners in regard to the matter just quoted. The leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) asked the other day whether the government intended to appoint anybody to represent these commissioners. Their action has been called into question, their finding has been challenged, the matter is referred to Judge Cassels, with the hope evidently that the findings of this commission will be reversed. Under such circumstances would it not seem honest and fair, Mr. Speaker, that instead of the gentleman whose department is attacked first selecting his own judge, them proceeding to try some of the offenders himself before the investigation could come on and then selecting two eminent counsel who are clearly identified with his party and with this department, somebody should have been appointed to represent Canada and to represent these gentlemen who have had the bravery to make this report to the government. The minister has seen fit to take Mr. LENNOX
another course. I have not a word to say against Judge Cassels.
But I have this to say-and I think I shall be upheld in the country if not in this House-that this whole affair is inconclusive. 1 venture the prediction that this trial will result in the same kind of farce as did the West Elgin election trial some years ago, in which also Mr. Watson figured. I say that, not because I have no faith in Judge Cassels-I have every faith in him;
I believe that if he were given a chance he would get at the bottom of this matter ; but I have pointed out that he is not given a chance ; he is bound by the terms of the order of reference in such a way that he cannot possibly investigate this matter as it ought to be investigated in the public interest. And this I say because the government has shown a desire to follow the methods of their friends in Ontario in the West Elgin case and their own methods in the insurance investigation of a more recent day. The minister says there must be a full and thorough investigation. But how is it to be accomplished ? Behind closed doors. A full and thorough investigation was promised when the insurance commission was appointed. But what happened ? The moment counsel appeared on behalf of parties interested, Judge MacTavish refused, at the instance of Mr. Shepley, to allow that counsel to ask a question. And the same method will be pursued in this investigation. Why should not counsel appear and have a statgs in this investigation ? Why should the doors be closed ? The officials of the department over wThich my hon. friend (Mr. Brodeur) presides, officials of whom he is the guardian in a sense, are attacked ; they are on trial. Yet, I venture to say that, with all his boasted sense of justice and his boasted desire for a full and fair investigation, he would not allow the counsel of these gentlemen to appear in order that a fair investigation may be held. A cloud may rest upon the officials, or it may rest upon those who are higher than the' officials. And, in that condition of things, is it fair-or is it not an outrage ?- to commit the matter to two counsel, one being Mr. Watson, who has been all his life identified with the workings of the Ross administration, and the other, this gentleman from Quebec, who is identified clearly and completely with the department under investigation, and both selected by my hon. friend (Mr. Brodeur) ? So, I have no hesitation in saying that this investigation will be a farce in its progress and a farce in its results.
Let us see how these things are worked out. Mr. Watson will be the senior counsel in this matter. I have nothing to say against him personally. So far as a man can be said to be a good man who is of his political persuasion and has always been mixed up with the managing of the machine,

he is a fairly good man. But I do not think that this kind of thing adds to a professional man's morality in the end. Mr. Watson is the gentleman who engineered the West Elgin election case, and he is the gentleman who will guide this proceeding. I do not think he will go as far as Mr. Shep-ley went in the insurance inquiry. Mr. Shepley was the counsel throughout the entire insurance investigation ; he guided and shaped the evidence, and every question by anybody else had to percolate through Mr. Shepley and he had to give his own interpretation to it in propounding it to the witness. And at the end, when all the evidence was in, you will say. Mr. Shepley, after addressing the commission, went about his business leaving them to decide. Nothing of the kind ; Mr. Shepley remained, as we have been told in this House to assist and direct the judges, before whom he had pleaded, in arriving at their conclusions. We shall have a better state of things, I believe, in this ease, for the reason that I have faith in Judge Cassels and feel sure that he will not consent to anything of that kind. But, still, we shall have an investigation guided by Mr. Watson. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Brodeur), in one breath told us that he had told Judge Cassels the other day that he was to have a full and thorough investga-tiou
That was gratuitous.

Yes. That he was to find out the guilty parties and spare them not. i But in the next breath, the minister tells us that it would be improper for him to instruct the judge as to what he should do. That is only in passing, however.) What I particularly want to point out is that the minister told us that Judge Cassels said he wished to have counsel to assist in this investigation. But he did not tell us-and so I assume it did not happen-that he asked Judge Cassels to name counsel that would suit him Oh, no ! that would not do. Counsel must be named by the very party that names the judge, the party that more than any other is interested in the final result of the investigation. In the West Elgin case, we have a confession signed by Donald McNish, and witnessed by A. B. Aylesworth, his counsel, of the state of things in that election. Subsequent to that, we had three judges appointed by the Ross administration to inquire into the manner of conducting that election, Judge Barron, Judge Morgan and Judge MaeTavish-and the last named qualified, more or less, I imagine, in that case for his subsequent employment at the instance of the Crown. And when 1 tell you that these judges say that practically nothing was done wrong in the West Elgin election, and when I read you the confession of their own side you will be able to form an opinion as to that
inquiry. That investigation was conducted and engineered by Mr. Watson. And the report, in concluding, compliments Mr. Watson upon the able and thorough manner in which he conducted the case on behalf of the Crown. I have here a speech made by Hon. Geo. W. Ross in which he refers to that trial and appears to think that Mr. Watson acted on behalf of the culprits, Pritchett and others, who were on trial. He said :
Mr. Watson had acted for the defence; he did so on his own responsibility.
But, to be perfectly fair, let me say that the hon. gentleman may have referred to the subsequent trial in which it happened that Mr. Watson, who had acted for the Crown in the first investigation, appeared for the defence. Either way is not satisfactory in some regards. However, Mr. Watson is complimented on the result of that investigation. Mr. Ross points out in a speech he made in Napanee on the eve of the last general elections, what a satisfactory result it was, and it was satisfactory in the face of what I am going to read to you, signed by Donald Macnish, the gentleman who produced and furnished unfair recommendations of the gentlemen to be deputy returniing officers, and that declaration was witnessed and concurred in by A. That a large number of persons were especially sent into the constituency by men working on behalf of the Liberal party for the express purpose of taking part on Mr. Maenish's behalf in the election held January 12, 1899, and we believe that fraudulent and corrupt means were used by some of such persons to secure his election.

I have only one word to say in addition. When that matter was subsequently referred to Judge Barron, Judge Morgan and Judge McTavish and they sat and examined 211 witnesses, as Mr. Ross here states in his speech at Napanee, and as the fact was, these gentlemen, under the able guidance of Mr. Watson, whom they complimented, were able so far to whitewash the illegality, rascality and criminality indulged in on that occasion, that they found practically that nothing wrong had been done in West Elgin.

I would not have risen to speak on this occasion were it not for some words that fell from the lips of the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster). It seems to me that the burden of what he said in regard to His Honour Judge Cassels, and the investigation before that commissioner, implies one of two things, either that he thinks the commissioner is dishonest or a fool. Whatever his oninion may be, I do not think that the members of this House imagine for a moment that His Honour Judge Cassels is either the one or the other. In fact, he was chosen by the government to carry on that investigation because we had absolute confidence in his integrity and his ability, and. therefore, we thought it better to leave the conduct of the investigation entirely in his hands. The commissioner asked for legal assistance and he has received it. He has not yet declared to us or to the country whether the investigation is to be an open one or in camera. I may say that the government assumed, and does still assume, that that investigation will be a public one, and the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) has absolutely no foundation whatever for his assumption that it is to be in camera ; he has absolutely no foundation for the fabric of accusations he has raised against the action of the government on that supposition. I will not say any more in regard to that, because I believe that the matter is in the hands of an absolutely competent and honest judge, and having put it into his hands we think it best to let him deal with it in the way he sees fit.

Before my hon. friend spoke, had the government decided in their own minds that it would be a good thing to have the investigation public?
Mr. FISHER
The government has not given any dictation to the commissioner.
Did the Minister of Marine and Fisheries know as much about it as the Minister of Agriculture, and if he did, why didn't he answer the question that was put to him?

All I say is that the matter has been left in the hands of the commission. We have assumed that the investigation will be public, but at the same time we. have not undertaken to dictate whether it shall be or not. I do not think that in any way contradicts what the Minister of Marine and Fisheries has said.
I cannot come to that conclusion.

My hon. friend may come to his own conclusions, but his own conclusions very often lead him stray, as they would lead the country astray if they were accepted. My hon. friend from North Toronto has talked about ministerial responsibility and about the responsibility of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries has assumed his full ministerial responsibility so far as regards the efficiency of the department, the organization and work of the department. But the minister has not assumed the duties of a judge to investigate the integrity and honesty of his officials. I do not think that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries is at all called upon to exercise that function, and if he had, on the report of the Civil Service Commission, undertaken to declare that so and so and so and so were dishonest and must be dealt with. hon. gentlemen opposite would have been the very first to raise a howl of partisanship and political persecution. It was because the Minister of Marine and Fisheries did not wish to assume the responsibility of prosecuting any of the gentlemen who were smirched by this report of the Civil Service Commission that the government appointed an independent judge who could do that in a judicial manner and without the slightest suspicion of partisanship.
The hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries has been very busy, ever since the acceptance of the position of minister, investigating his department. He has been trying to use his ministerial responsibility to put that department on a firmer and more satisfactory footing. What has been the history of my hon. colleague the Minister of Marine and Fisheries since he has become minister ? He took that office, I think, in February, 1906. He was in the midst of an arduous session, he carried through the work of that session, and the parliamentary duties of a minister absolutely precluded his making a thorough investigation into the details of the working of his department. Immediately after the session he sat-

isfied himself that the book-keeping of the .department was not all it ought to be, and he then employed Mr. Falconer to undertake a thorough investigation of the book-keeping of the department, not only to try to find out whether there was any absolute wrong-doing, but to find whether a better system of accounting could not be adopted and put into operation. The evidence of Sir. Falconer and the other accountants who came before the Committee on Public Accounts showed that it required time not only to investigate but to work out a system which they might substitue for the system which was in existence before they began their work. My hon. friend the Minister of Marine spent the summer going about the country examining and investigating the different offices of the department. He came back here in the fall to enter upon a long and arduous session during which it was impossible for him, with his parliamentary duties, to undertake a thorough investigation. At the close of the session of 1907 he was called upon by the Prime Minister, at the request of the imperial government, to go to England and take part in the colonial conference. While he was there he was asked by the Prime Minister to help my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) in the negotiation of the French treaty and he was away for six months. During that time he could not carry on any investigation or reorganization of the department. When he came back he asked for the report of Mr. Falconer and in a little while afterwards he had the report of the Civil Service Commission. But, before the report of the Civil Service Commission had come to him or to the government my hon. friend had commenced again, on his ministerial responsibility, an investigation into the organization of his department with the object of bringing about efficiency in the service and which it is his duty to carry on and which is not a matter at all for the investigation which Judge Cassels has been asked to undertake. My hon. friend (Mr. Foster) spoke a few minutes ago as if the investigation which has now been entrusted to Judge Cassels ought to have been carried on by the Civil Service Commissioners. The Civil Service Commissioners, as a matter of fact, did not make any accusations against any individuals, although they did make general statements in regard to conditions in the department. X have not spoken to the commissioners about it. but from their report I should say that they did not consider that they were the proper persons to conduct a judicial investigation and take evidence in regard to the particular responsibility or honesty of any one member of the department. We have put it into the hands of a judge who is the right man to make a judicial investigation and give a judicial decision. My hon. friend (Mr. Foster) spoke of the accusations in the
Civil Service Commissioners report. If they had made any accusations surely they would not be the right people to investigate and give a decision on the question in regard to which they had made accusations. If Judge Cassels thinks it wise he can summon the Civil Service Commissioners before him to give any further information than that published in the report and we can get the advantage of that. I had not intended to dilate upon these matters. I am not going into details with regard to them at all. There will be occasions upon which they can be taken up and dealt with at greater length. I only want to show that the accusations which have been made against my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries are not well founded. Those against my hon. friend in regard to his shirking his' ministerial responsibility are not justified or based upon facts, but, as a matter of, fact, the action and the career of my hon. friend, since he has assumed that office, show that in every possible way he has been prepared to take the responsibility of his ministerial position although he is not prepared to take the judicial action of deciding whether an individual officer in his department is guilty of dishonesty or not. He leaves that to a gentleman whose reputation is such that hon. members on the other side of the House cannot, in so many words, attack it, although they may try to insinuate that he may be influenced unworthily.
