Mr. Speaker, with all deference to those who have spoken on the other side of the House, it seems to me that in this discussion they have strayed far from the questions which the leader of the opposition so courteously asked the First Minister this afternoon. There were two simple questions put to the right hon. gentleman. One was, why the inquiry in this case had been restricted and placed under the second part of the Act respecting public and departmental inquiries instead of under the first part of that Act; and the other inquiry was, whether, in addition to the two Liberal partisan counsel who would defend the government, it was the intention of the government to appoint other counsel who would act independently in the interests of the people of Canada at large. If I can understand the reasons given by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries in relation to the first question put by the leader of the opposition, he takes the ground that he himself and the government had in no way been attacked by the report of this commission, that he and the government are held absolutely

blameless and that therefore there is no necessity for any inquiry of a general character in the public interest. The Minister of Finance also seems to state that while there may be and no doubt is a constitutional responsibility there is no further or other responsibility falling upon the government which would involve inquiry into anything except the conduct of some officials whose names have not been mentioned in the report of the Civil Service Commission. That must indeed be a very comforting position for the government to take. They congratulate themselves that they are absolutely absolved and held guiltless, and they therefore decide they will have no tribunal to Investigate themselves, but they will have an investigation of some of the departmental officials. Let me present to the government and its followers some few considerations which they may reasonably think on before they become steadfast in their conclusion as to their non-responsibility in this matter, and as to the interest of the public in a broad investigation instead of the restricted and narrow investigation which they offer. It is interesting to note that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries declares that he wants the fullest possible investigation and that while he holds up one hand for the fullest possible investigation he holds up the other hand for a narrow and restricted inquiry into the officials of his department only.' That is a contrast which the people of this country are quite able to appreciate. The Minister of Finance told us that in 1892 Civil Service Commission made a report which to a large extent involved some of the various iniquities which the present civil service report has pointed out. If that be correct, then I do charge that the government of this country from 1896 to the present time have been going on in the full knowledge that these double prices were being paid and in the knowledge of the iniquities which have been proven by this new Civil Service Commission. Even if that were not so, I charge that the question of this department and all the mismanagement and all the extravagance of this department was brought up in this House two years ago by the leader of the opposition who on May 18, 1906, moved :
That all the words after the word ' that ' in the proposed motion he omitted and the following substituted therefor:
A committee of seven members be appointed to inquire into and investigate the expenditure of public moneys in or by the Department of Marine and Fisheries from and after the 30th day of June. 1902, and to inquire whether any abuses, irregularities, improvidences or maladministrations have arisen or occurred in respect of such expenditures and whether any persons employed in oi' connected with the said department have profited therebv. and whether any additional safeguards _ should be provided in respect of the expenditure of public money in or by the Mr. BRISTOL.
said department and to report upon the matters aforesaid.
That the said committee have power to send for persons, papers and records and to examine witnesses under oath.
By means of this resolution and the speeches in support of it, the government had their attention brought in the most forceful manner to the absolute rottenness of the administration of this department, and it is idle for them now to say they have no responsibility. Two years ago when this resolution was moved, everybody who takes an intelligent interest in the public affairs of Canada was well aware of the rottenness of this department, and yet the government wilfully shut their eyes to it or were incompetent to apply a remedy. There was brought to the attention of the government at this time the scandal of the ' Arctic,' the scandal of the purchase of cutlery for the ' Montcalm ' where the most extraordinary prices were paid for tableware for an ice-breaker, and above all there were the Merwin scandals. I emphasize this latter because in the Public Accounts Committee in 1906 it was proven that this man Merwin had sold to the Department of Marine and Fisheries, articles which that department and any business man in this country could have purchased direct from the wholesale merchants and manufacturers at from 100 to 187 per cent less than they paid Merwin. There was a Sturtevant engine which cost $262.50 and which was sold to the department by Merwin for $550: there was another engine of a similar character which cost $25 and was sold to the department for $550, and another similar engine which cost $335 and which was sold to the department for $900 or at a profit on the transaction of 187 per cent. The battle was fought in the Public Accounts Committee in respect to this man Merwin and it was only after the greatest possible effort and in face of obstruction on the part of members on the other side of the House that the facts in relation to this thing were brought out. I.et me ask? Is there any sane business man on the opposite side or any sane business man in Canada, who, if he found a man charging him an exorbitant profit or from 100 per cent to 187 per cent for articles of ordinary commerce, would go on buying from that man without tender and without having his prices checked. But that state of affairs went on until October last, and goods were purchased from Merwin to the extent of considerably over a million dollars without tender. And yet the government say :	We are a
business administration and we have no responsibility in this matter. Why, Sir, if the board of directors of any company were to tell the shareholders that for three years they had gone on dealing with a man who had so grossly overcharged them for ordinary articles, the management of that com-

pany would not be permitted to continue for a moment. Surely, the administration of the public affairs of a country should certainly be on the same business basis as the administration of the affairs of a private commercial corporation. Nay more, X would put it on a higher plane, and 1 would say that a man of honour anxious to endeavour to live up to the fullest extent to the trust imposed in him, would be even more careful in the conduct of a great public department than in the ordinary affairs of business.
Here we have the spectacle of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, for over two years in this department, with statements brought constantly to his attention as to the rottenness of that department, saying and the government saying : We knew nothing of this matter ; we are not responsible ; the commissioners have found no fault with us, let us go after a few understrappers in the department. I think the people of this country will not be satisfied with such sophistry ; business men, who conduct their affairs honestly, will not be satisfied with such an absurd and unintelligible argument put forward by the apologists of this government. Mr. Speaker, I want to place on record the plain distinction between the two classes of investigation which are open to the administration. In the first place, they appointed a commission in May, 1907. not to investigate charges or abuses, irregularities, improvidence or mal-administration, but to look into the operation of the Civil Service Act and the services and compensation of the officials of the government ; and such inquiry was to include the following subjects :
1.	General operation of the Civil Service
Act.	.
2.	Classification of the service.
3.	Salaries.
4.	Temporary employment.
5.	Technical employees.
6.	Promotions.
7.	Discipline, hours of service, &c.
8.	Efficiency and sufficiency of the departmental staffs.
9.	Retiring allowances.
10.	Any other matter relative to th© service which in the opinion of the commissioners requires consideration.
It has been pointed out that two bon. ministers have attacked these commissioners for going outside of the terms of their commission ; and if it had not been for clause 10, it would no doubt have been possible legally to take that position ; but under clause 10 they had the right, and they exercised that right, of making a more general investigation. Now, the order in council authorizing that commission was passed under part 1 section 2 of an Act respecting public and departmental inquiries, being chapter 104 of the Revised Statutes of Canada. Subsection 2 is as follows:
The Governor in Council may. whenever he deems it expedient, cause inquiry to be made into and concerning any matter connected with the good government of Canada or the conduct of any part of the public business thereof.
The order in council appointing the Hon. Mr. Justice Cassels as commissioner is based on part 2, section (i, of the same Act, relating to departmental investigations, which read as follows:
The minister presiding over any department of the Civil Service of Canada may appoint at any time, under the authority of the Governor in Council, a commissioner or commissioners to investigate and report upon the state and management of the business or any part of the business of such department, either in the inside or outside service thereof, and the conduct of any person in such service, so far as the same relates to his official duties.'
The part which the Hou. Mr. Justice Cassels has been asked to investigate is merely one statement in the report, which is as follows :
That immediate steps should be taken in order to determine what officials, if any, deserve condemnation, and to give to all an opportunity to meet the charges implied.
By the very terms of this last commission the minister and the government leave themselves out of the investigation. Suppose the investigation goes on. Certain officials of the department are charged with getting graft or commissions, and the question is naturally asked, what did the minister know of these transactions ? Did you tell him or give him information of the people from whom you were buying, or of the high prices you were paying ? Under this commission questions of this kind are completely shut out, because the conduct of the minister is in no way to be inquired into ; the inquiry is absolutely confined, under the order in council, to the acts of certain officials of the department. So that we have the administration calmly saying, in the light of the facts which are common knowledge to the people of this country ; although for years we have known of these charges of graft, and although within the last two years they have been brought repeatedly to our attention, we are absolutely without responsibility, we are innocent, there is no charge against us.
Now, I do not wish again to go over the very able argument which was made by my hon. friend from East Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) in regard to the responsibility of the minister ; but I do affirm that any unprejudiced person, reading that report, will say, quite apart from any observations that I have addressed to the House, that there is ample evidence on which any man wishing to protect his honour against aspersions, any government holding themselves high as the guardians and trustees of the people, would have demanded the fullest possible investi-

gation and the fullest opportunity to free themselves of any suspicion of connection with or knowledge of the graft that is [DOT]charged. And so I submit that when it is sought to narrow this investigation, it is an absolute and direct effort on the part of the administration to contract themselves [DOT]out of the investigation and to say :	We
are innocent, we do not propose to have any inquiry made into our acts, but we propose to narrow the inquiry down to what a few officials in the department may or may not have done.
That leads up to the second point which is of great importance to the people of this [DOT]country, and that is the method of conduct [DOT]of this investigation. And here one is somewhat amused at the answers which have been made to-day ; because, instead of the -ministers making a fair and proper answer to the questions of the lion, leader of the [DOT]opposition and the arguments advanced, they put up straw men and at once *knock them down. A very good example of that was the argument presented this afternoon by the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher), who tried to insinuate that some attack had been made by this side of the House upon the hon. Mr. Justice 'Cassels as the commissioner in this inquiry. I want to say, so far as I have the right to *do so, that I have not heard any such attack, i do not believe that any such attack was directly or indirectly made, and I want to be allowed to say that I have known the Hon. Mr. Justice Cassels for many years, and I gladly say that he is universally regarded by the bar of Ontario as one [DOT]of our ablest lawyers and one of our most high-minded and impartial men. I cannot pay too high a tribute to the great abilities of that hon. gentleman, and I do not think the government could have made a better [DOT]choice for their commissioner than the hon. judge whom they have appointed, and that is the feeling, so far as I know it, on the [DOT]Conservative side of this House. But that has nothing to do with the question. That was simply to draw a red herring across the trail. The hon. Minister of Finance attempted to make an excuse for the appointment of two partisan Liberal counsel to assist in this investigation ; and when it was pointed out to him that when a charge was made against a Conservative department, two of the ablest Liberal lawyers in Canada, one of English origin and one of French origin, were appointed to assist in the investigation, the Minister of Finance said, in that case it was a Tory minister who was involved, whereas in this case it was merely the officials of the department. It certainly is a -new distinction to make that we should employ the most distinguished counsel to bring to earth a Conservative minister, while we should employ a partisan counsel to bring to justice, if justice it be, the members of a department who have been accused of wrong-doing.

That, of course, is an absolutely and utterly illogical position for the Minister of Finance or any one else to take. The whole point is : Do hon. gentlemen opposite really think they will have satisfied their own honour, will have satisfied their Liberal friends throughout the country, will have satisfied public opinion in Canada by appointing to assist in this matter two strongly biased Liberal lawyers It does not matter how able they are, the point that was made is simply that it would be common decency, at all events, if the government proposed to appoint two gentlemen of the same stripe of politics as the administration whose life, so to speak, is at stake in this matter, to have appointed independent counsel who were not strongly swayed by considerations of party politics.
I wish to emphasize, with all the force I can, what I believe to be the indecency, and impropriety of this administration in appointing these two gentlemen to act as counsel. It goes to show that the ingenuous and somewhat amusing, but I fancy hardly intentional statement of the Minister of Marine to-day that he did not want any blame to attach to himself or to the government in connection with this matter, was really to be worked out by the fact first that the new commission was so restricted that it was absolutely impossible under its terms to attack either the minister or the government, and secondly that counsel were being employed whose political proclivities were such that it might reasonably be anticipated that their bias would induce them to do every thing they could to protect the government by whom they were paid and whose life long supporters they were. So, Mr. Speaker, in conclusion I wish to protest as strongly and as vigorously as I can against both the restricted nature of this commission and the appointment of partisan council in connection with the investigation of a matter of such great public importance.

speakeroldname: Hon. A. B. AYLESWORTH (Minister of Justice).
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the subject under discussion may be, I suppose, compendiously stated as whether or not this government has done right in the course it has taken in this matter in authorizing the issue of a commission to Mr. Justice Cassels. To appreciate whether or not that action on the part of the government was the correct method of dealing with this subject, it seems to me we should remember exactly the position created by the circumstance of the report of the Civil Service Commission being made and laid on the table of this House. I do not, for the moment. speak of the circumstance that no sooner was that report presented, no sooner had it become the subject of any discussion in this House, than the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) who to-day inveighs so emphatically against the course

the government has taken in this matter, was himself the very first to suggest that it was incumbent on the government to deal with this question either by the appointment of a committee of this House or by the issue of some commission of inquiry. \\ e have taken the better of these two alternatives. I do not suppose any hon. gentleman in this House would contend that any more impartial tribunal for the investigation of this question could by possibility have been selected than the one which has been named or that there would have been any greater propriety, even although there had been party advantage, in the appointment of a committee of this House to investigate this question. We have then accepted and acted on one of the two alternative suggestions made by the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster), yet in doing that it seems we have, according to the views he has expressed to-day, most grievously erred. It is of course but another example of the facility with which hon. gentlemen who desire to criticise on all occasions the government of the day and who are determined, no matter what course that government may take, to condemn it off-hand, and to cry out against the course which it has adopted, will trim their sails according to the breeze and be prepared at any time and In any event and at all seasons to condemn whatever may be done by those who are opposed to them politically. The situation when this report from the commission of inquiry into the operation of the civil service was made was, it seems to me, a very simple and plain one. I have been accused to-day of having attacked this commission when speaking-before my constituents on the subject some three or four weeks ago. I deny that statement ; X made no attack. If I had wanted to criticise, the material for criticism was ready to my hand. I did not even criticise, although the report of the commission itself certainly well invited criticism. X said on that occasion what I have no hesitation in saying again and w'hat any hon. gentleman who reads the mandate to these commissioners can at once see for himself, namely, that they stepped altogether outside of that which was defined to them as their jurisdiction when they made a report at length as they have made with regard to the different departments of the governmental service. They were appointed to inquire into the operation of the Civil Service Act; they were not appointed to inquire into the administration of the general departments of the government service. They were appointed with specific reference to many matters arising under the Civil Service Act. These particular matters were specified in the order in council appointing them, in the commission issued to them. They were to inquire generally into the operation of the statute, with special reference to the
classification of the service, to the salaries of the service, to the matter of temporary employment, of technical employment, of promotions, of discipline, of the hours of service, of retiring allowances and then (in the only phrase that could possibly, by any stretch, be taken to cover the course which they followed in making the remarks they have seen fit to make on general administration) they were finally appointed to inquire into the efficiency and sufficiency of the departmental staffs. I am not here to criticise, much less to attack the course which the commissioners took. I am simply pointing out, not in any way of attack or even of criticism upon their work, that they did undoubtedly go beyond the commission of inquiry issued to them in what they have reported. But that I make no point of, that is in no degree an answer to what they have said, or in any way a circumstance which relieved the government from considering the report which they have seen fit to make. When that report comes to be presented not only does it deal with matters committed to them for inquiry, but it goes into the general question of the administration of the different departments of the government service, and they have reported to this House that in the Department of Marine and Fisheries there is this to be criticised, the system in vogue of distributing the daily correspondence of the department. They have taken the time to discuss at some length that method of distributing the correspondence and to suggest what they consider would be improvements in it. They next take up and discuss what they say is a lack of efficient organization in the staff of that department, and at considerable length again they discuss that feature of the administration of the department. Other similar matters are dealt with, with which the minister who is in charge of that department, himself can deal, and in regard to which he is himself engaged. But they have gone further and have not only stated these general things with regard to the administration, the organization and the system or method of doing the work of that department by the staff there employed, but have said that there seems also to be in that department a lack of conscience, and having made that statement they follow it up by saying that some government officials are serving two masters. That is a tolerably specific statement, if we can make that observation with regard to something that is absolutely and entirely general. I do not know, I have very considerable doubt in my own mind, whether the gentleman who penned that phrase had at the time or has now any certain, particular person in mind toward whom he aimed when he used the expression :	There are some of the government
officials who are serving two masters.
I incline to think, after giving it the best

consideration I am able, that the gentleman who used these words himself would say-I did not mean any specific person ; I meant merely, in arguing what I thought must be the condition of things, to say that, from what I had seen of the lack of organization-of the lack of efficient work, if you please, of the wrong system upon which things are done in that department- there must be somebody or other who was serving two masters. Now, whichever thing he meant-whether the man who wrote those words meant that there was some particular individual or set of individuals in the department who were lacking in conscience and who were trying to serve not merely their employers but some one else from whom they were receiving benefits for favours given, whichever meaning was attached, in the mind of the person who wrote these words, to the words he has used, it is a subject of inquiry. And I do not for a moment shirk the situation that, although this was something quite beyond what these commissioners were appointed to do, the fact that they have said it is, none the less, a reason why the thing which they have said must of necessity have, at the hands of the government, further investigation.
Now, it seems to me that the circumstance presented by the delivery of that report from any person entrusted by the Crown in any kind of inquiry into a matter affecting the public service was not unlike, in principle, what would be the case supposing some party of government surveyors or some set of men who might be in government employment and sent out on some prospecting investigation, came, if you like, by accident-or, if you like, by search -upon a dead body in the course of their work. and. looking at the circumstances, thought that this dead body might have been the result of foul play and. in the course of their report upon their work made the observation that they had, upon a certain day, come upon this corpse, and that there might have been foul play in connection with it. What then would be done ? What would be the duty of those charged with the administration of justice, without regard to whether this body of men had been sent out for the purpose of searching for what they had found, or had come upon it, and had reported that they had come upon it. by accident? The course naturally taken wTOuld be the empanelling of a coroner's jury, and the investigation of this corpus delicti by the form of a coroner's inquest. That is exactly the course the government has taken in this matter. Hon. members in this House talk about somebody being on trial. The very men who use that expression over and over and over again must perfectly understand that this is no proceeding in the nature of a charge and trial, that it is nothing else than that to which I have likened it, an examin-Mr. AYLESWORTH.
ation into circumstances-of, if you like, a suspicious character-in regard to which an investigation is directed precisely of the nature which is carried on by a coroner and coroner's jury in the case of inquest upon a body found. In these circumstances this is in no sense a prosecution or trial; it is an investigation to ascertain facts. This report gives no one any facts upon which he can act. Merely by way of illustration, I presume, two instances are given of what the commissioners say they found in the nature of impropriety or wrong-doing in the department; and, as I said before, if one wanted to go looking for opportunity of criticism, it would not be hard to find material ready to hand upon the face of this report itself. Because, it turns out, the moment they mention in detail two specific instances of what they thought was wrong-doing in the department, in each of the two cases it was they who were mistaken and the department was absolutely correct. They charge, in terms, that there had been an authorization by the department, that there had been an accepting by the minister, of a recommendation of one of his subordinates, to depart from a contract and to pay a higher price for a certain commodity than that which the seller had undertaken to receive. In that, they were entirely wrong. They fell into an error, not unnaturally, but an error which they would not have fallen into if any one had known that they were travelling outside the purpose for which they were appointed or were engaged in an investigation which they intended to make the foundation of a report of this character-which simply illustrates the danger of acting upon or accepting the conclusions of gentlemen who have gone about a work which they were not appointed to undertake, and a work which nobody was aware they were engaged in at all. If they had mentioned to anybody in the department, I suppose, that they thought there wTas in these circumstances of the coal purchase at Prescott something that called for explanation, any official of the department acquainted with the facts, or in possession of the files of the department, could at once have shown them that, in that particular instance at all events, there was nothing calling for comment, for the minister at the head of the department, immediately on the recommendation of his subordinate coming to his attention, refused to act upon it, directed that the contract should be acted upon and that that thing exactly should be done which the commissioners find fault writh the department because they thought it was not done. In the other instance, they are equally at sea, and equally under a mistake, simply by reason of the circumstance that they were going on unguided, unassisted, and without reference to any person who was in a position to know the facts and drawing conclusions which the

circumstances not only did not warrant, but, immediately on being known, demonstrated were entirely at variance with the truth.
Now, notwithstanding that these features of the report must necessarily lessen the weight which otherwise would be attached to it, we have the fact that two out of the three gentlemen for this purpose make these observations with regard to the personnel of the staff in the Department of Marine and Fisheries. What was the government to do ? I make no point of the fact that the third or chief commissioner did not concur in the remarks of his colleagues. It would have been exactly the same situation if but one of the three commissioners had said what the two have said here. If, instead of saying it in the report, they had said it by letter, or in any formal way had brought It to the attention of the government or of the minister, the situation would have been identically the same ; and therefore, I say, I make no point whatever of the fact that they have travelled afield and outside and beyond their jurisdiction; I make no point whatever in derogation of the weight that should be attached to this report of the other circumstances I have adverted to. I come simply down to this situation, that gentlemen who were entrusted by the government with a certain investigation have seen things, in the course of that investigation which, they say, call for further inquiry, and that they considered themselves justified in summing up by the statement that somebody or other in the Department of Marine and Fisheries was without conscience and apparently serving two masters. That is the one thing in the report that calls for further action in the nature of inquiry. The other things in the report are matters of departmental administration with which the minister is in a position to deal. But that particular statement is a statement which cannot be ignored and a statement in regard to which no investigation the minister himself could make would satisfy hon. gentlemen who are so ready to criticise that nothing whatever which can be done will satisfy them. That statement appearing on the face of the report was something which, according to the gentleman who, for the time being, was leading the opposition, called for the issue of a further commission of inquiry, or the appointment of a committee of this House to investigate; and the government taking the view which he presented, has appointed a further commission of inquiry to do exactly the work which I have described as the work of a coroner and a coroner's jury in this matter. , Well, the next question I suppose is whether any exception can be taken to the gentleman who is chosen for the duty. Now I am not aware that any person in this House or out of it has taken the slightest exception to the gentleman who has been
named to do this work. We have in the past not only, in this House but in other legislative assemblies in this country, seen the' necessity arise for the appointment of commissions of inquiry of one character or another. We in the province of Ontario, within the last three years, have seen a good many instances of it, and we have seen commissions of inquiry appointed by a government supported by hon. gentlemen who sit opposite, a government that they laud to the skies and we have seen commission after commission issued by that government to political heelers of the very lowest description, selected for no other purpose than to do the duty of an executioner, and in whose hands the result of the commission was foreseen and expected. If this government had selected for the purpose of this inquiry a man as commissioner against whom one word of exception c-ould be taken, then there might have been some foundation for the attacks that have been made today, and that have been made consistently since this commission was appointed ; as if there was in the appointment some intention to whitewash, some intention to prevent thoroughness, some intention to get over what is said to be the damaging effects of the commissioners' report. I say Sir, that the very fact that this gentleman has been chosen as commissioner is in itself a sufficient answer to charges of that character.
But criticism upon the course of the government does not stop there. Criticism fol- . lows the least action which is taken by the government, objection is sure to follow every step which the government may take, no matter what it may be. If the hon. the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, instead of making the appointment he has made, had chosen to investigate for himself and had made no appointment of a commissioner at all, it would at once have been said that he was standing behind his officials, that he was identifying himself with them, that if they were without conscience, as was charged by the commissioners, then he was equally to be condemned because he was making common cause with them. On the other hand, the moment that he appointed this commission of inquiry, at once the word went out from headquarters, at once the ' Mail ' newspaper, which I suppose is the gospel of the hon. gentlemen from the province of Ontario who sit opposite, takes the position that the minister has determined to sacrifice his subordinates, that he is not manly enough to stand behind them, but that the fiat has gone forth that they must be beheaded. Well, everyone is prepared for either alternative, that is a beautiful example at all events of the fact that whatever course may be taken in this matter by the government, that course will necessarily be condemned, and that course is the one which will afford the best opportunity for criticism and attack.

Now, Sir, the commissioner having been selected, and being a gentleman not only above reproach, but actually above even attack by those who would attack every earthly thing that was done by this government, the next question was as to the manner in which that inquiry should be carried on. Now it has been said that the commissioner himself desired in this matter to have the assistance of council. I take no advantage of that position. I assume, as legal adviser if you please of the government in this matter, the ful'est responsibility upon my own shoulders for the advice that this was an inquiry which ought not to be conducted without tlie assistance of counsel ; and whether the commissioner desired council or not, I would certainly be unwilling that he should enter upon an inquiry of this character, one the result of which is so certain to be attacked, without the help of counsel to assist in the investigation, and relieve him from some portion of the laborious work which otherwise he would have to undertake personally. Somebody of necessity must investigate, case after case of individual character; somebody must pore through file after file, thousands upon thousands of pages in the Department of Marine and Fisheries ; somebody must of necessity go up many a blind alley before he can possibly hit upon anything that would be productive of results, anything that could lead to a determination of any of the circumstances whi.cli the commissioner is appointed to investigate. It might be said :	Let
the commissioner himself do it. His time is no more valuable than that of anybody else ; he is a public servant, and let him take the weeks or months that may be necessary' to do that work of preliminary investigation. I submit that it would not be wise or prudent that the commissioner should do that work, and for the simple reason that the man, whoever he is, who does that work of investigation, whoever he is. whether counsel or commissioner, who does the work of questioning witnesses, must and will be undoubtedly represented as prosecuting counsel. This inquiry although it is in every sense as far removed from the trial of any accusation as any inquiry possibly could be, is already represented by nearly every speaker opposite who has addressed you to-day, as a trial of somebody or other, and just as it is so improperly represented, just as it is sought to be in the eyes of the people so distorted from its real character, so truly would the man who was conducting that inquiry, whether he were commissioner or counsel, be represented as nothing else but a prosecutor, or indeed a persecutor. The moment you put the commissioner into a position where it is possible to say that of him. you detract immeasurably from the weight which his report would have, and you at once bring him into the arena of a prosecuting counsel instead of leaving him Mr. AYLESWORT^
where he ought to be, a judicial officer to determine. In these circumstances I certainly felt no hesitation whatever in advising that counsel should be engaged for the assistance of the commissioner. I take upon myself the fullest responsibility for the course the government has taken, and am willing to relieve the commissioner absolutely from the suspicion even of having suggested that anything of the kind should be done.
Then it having been decided that there should be counsel in this matter, the next question was who that counsel should belt is perhaps not unnatural that, having the duty' of recommending the person of the counsel, I should turn in my mind at once to the men of my own immediate acquaintance. I happen to be, from the circumstance that for nearly a generation I have practised law in the city of Toronto, better acquainted with the lawyers of Toronto than I am with the lawyers of any other part of this country', and it was, in these circumstances, not an unnatural thing that I should canvass in my own mind the men with whom I am best acquainted and of whose ability and standing I have the best knowledge when it was a question of who should be selected for this work. I take the full responsibility of having recommended the name of Mr. Watson for this position. I did that upon my knowledge of the man, and I have not heard as yet any criticism offered except the question which I see was propounded by the hon. member for East Hastings (Mr. Northrop) as to Mr.- Watson's identity a few days ago, and the observation made this afternoon by the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) that he had been, or, I think, the statement was that he at the present time was in charge of the Liberal organization for the city of Toronto. Mr. Speaker, I am in a position to give an unqualified denial to the latter of these two statements. Mr. Watson is not, so far as I am aware, identified wi,th any Liberal organization in Toronto or elsewhere in this country. He was at one time, I think, chairman or president-I really do not know what the title was-of some organization of that character in Toronto-I have no idea whether for a riding or for a ward or for the whole city. I am absolutely indifferent on that head. I know Mr. Watson to be a Liberal politically'. He is a man who I know has confidence in me and perhaps it is not strange on that account that I should have confidence in him, and I do not hesitate in this House or anywhere in this country to justify before hon. members or before any body of men the selection of Mr. Watson for this work. He is a man of standing in his profession. I have known him personally for about 35 years, from the time when he was a struggling young barrister to the day' when he stands amongst the foremost leaders of the bar in the province of Ontario, and hon. gentleman must

recognize him not merely as a man of integrity and character, but as a man possessing legal attainments such as fit him for any brief or any work which may be entrusted to him by any client. In these circumstances I had no hesitation, on Mr. Watson occurring to my mind, to recommend him as a man who would conduct this inquiry properly, who would conduct it as it should be conducted, who would pursue the end towards which this investigation was directed and who would make the investigation of that thorough and complete character which was from the beginning intended. I cannot too highly emphasize the observation that was made this afternoon by my hon. colleague in charge of the Department of Marine and Fisheries, that the one intention and desire in the appointment of this commission was that this work should be thorough and the one piece of instruction which I have given in this matter to Mr. Watson in a personal interview and in writing was that this work was to be of a thorough character, that the thing that was expected of him was that he would spare no effort to make this investigation perfect and complete and that he would go into the department to the [DOT] very bottom of things and satisfy this government and the country whether or no there was any foundation for the remarks which have been made by the commission as to the lack of personal honesty and integrity on the part of officials of the department, and if there is foundation for them to determine who the men are that they may be weeded out from among their fellows and that the truth in regard to them may become known. These are the instructions that Mr. Watson has, and I am well enough acquainted with him to know that these instructions will be carried out and that the work which he undertakes will be work that is thoroughly done. In these circumstances it is not a subject of criticism, it is not a matter in regard to which those who may wish to criticise have the slightest ground for the attacks they make; that counsel has been selected anil that counsel has been the man of whom I have spoken.
Now, Sir, it has been asked here whether or not this gentleman is counsel for the minister or whether or not any counsel is to be engaged for the gentlemen who have prepared the report of the commission of inquiry into the civil service. Well, Sir, I scarcely know whether or not such a question is being propounded seriously. I suppose that the hon. gentleman who put such a question knows perfectly well the character of this investigation. If any hon. gentleman of the legal profession or acquainted with the ordinary course of legal proceedings puts such a question he must see at once that it carries with it its own answer. He knows-he must know that this investigation is in no sense, as I have already
said, a question of trying anybody, but that it is simply an investigation of inquiry, and he might quite as well ask, to return, again to the illustration which I have used before, whether or not counsel for somebody or other for some individual or witness, was going to appear before a coroner appointed to take evidence in an inquiry of this nature. It is no attack upon the commissioners, it is no trial of the commissioners, the commissioners are in no sense upon the defensive ; it is supplementing and. carrying forward the work which they, in the way in which I have described, have done. It is in no sense a review or a trial or any kind of imputation or charge against these commissioners. This, Sir, is simply a public inquiry and counsel who appear in this matter under the instructions of this government appear for the public, as occupying precisely the position that a county Crown attorney occupies at a coroner's ininquest, inquiring for the whole country and engaged to probe the matter to its depths to ascertain what foundation there may be for a statement which appears in the report which is the basis of this inquiry. Mr. Watson is counsel for the people. Hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House amuse themselves by using that phrase of which they are so fond, and I wonder if it never occurs to them that they are, perhaps, unconsciously, or perhaps purposely, seeking to identify the sixty or seventy men who compose His Majesty's opposition with the people of this country. They seem to forget that the people are represented by their chosen representatives in this House of parliament, that the country is represented by this government and that it is the government and not the gentleman who, sit on your left, Sir, who have the right to speak for the people in whom the people have time and time again already demonstrated, as time and time again they will in the future, demonstrate their confidence by their votes at the polls. Mr. Watson is the representative counsel in this inquiry for the people of this country. He is selected for that work by the government who have the confidence of this House and the confidence of the country, and it is of little moment for hon. gentlemen in whom so often the people of Canada have refused to repose confidence to speak here as though they were voicing the sentiments of the people of this country. I submit to you, Sir, under these circumstances that the appointment of Mr. Watson is one with which the people of Canada will be satisfied, and until some charge is brought against him other than that he belongs politically to the majority, his appointment is not open to criticism.
Now, I simply took the floor to speak as to the appointment of counsel. I regret that I am quite unable to answer observations that have been made in the course of this debate because I have had to depend en-

tirely on wliat good friends who are able i to hear have told me as to what has been | said. Unfortunately for myself I am not .physically in a position to engage in political controversy. I have risen simply to lay before the House the considerations which have moved the government to take the course it has taken in appointing for this important work the gentleman who has been selected as commissioner. I take great comfort to myself, as I am sure every one in this House ought to take comfort to himself, that the appointment of Mr. Justice Cassels has been so well received on all hands and that there has been no criticism applied to his appointment. Under these circumstances, whatever else may be said of this commission or of any person w7ho may be engaged in it, I have the confident hope that the course which that commissioner may take will commend itself to every one in this House and in the country. He can certainly be relied upon to do his duty in the premises, without fear, favour, partiality. or affection. He is acting literally in judicial capacity ; he is charged to report who the men are (if there be any) who are described in this portion of the report in .question. No other duty is put upon him nor was there any intention to put any other duty upon him. It is tacitly assumed that there is no such thing; but the whole commercial world knows otherwise. If no one gets any benefit from trade with the government except the trader, then it must be clear that in these great purchases made for the government without discount, its offi-

cers must be assisting the trader to get better prices from the government than he can get anywhere else; for everywhere else he has to get discount. In other words, some of the government's officers are serving two masters, and apparently succeeding with both-[DOT] scripture notwithstanding.
And the minister draws, in his report to council the inference that commissions are received improperly or that enhanced prices are paid through dishonesty on the part of officials in the Department of Marine and Fisheries. The report continues :	*
But unfortunately the report does not mention any names which would enable him to take definite action concerning these officials. It is, however, in the interest of the Department of Marine and Fisheries and of the country that immediate steps should be taken in order to determine what officials, if anv, deserve condemnation and to give to all an opportunity to meet the charges implied.
I submit that the statement is broad and generous. It draws the only inference that can be drawn. It is by way of reflection upon the officials of the department. I do not know whether my hon. friends, ingenious as they are in being able to manufacture imputations and suggest all kinds of wrong-doing without the slightest pretext can possibly infer more, from the language used, than what is indicated by the minister in his report, It seems to me that it gives full effect and to the utmost limit to which my hon. friends might go in that direction. What then does the minister do ?
The minister therefore recommends that he be authorized to appoint the Hon. Walter Cassels a commissioner under part 2 of chapter 104 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1906, to investigate and report upon the foregoing statements contained in the said report of the Civil Service Commission reflecting upon the integrity of the officials of the Department of Marine and Fisheries, or any of them.
That is the reference. Now, what can the gentleman who was appointed commissioner do? He is appointed under a section of the statute which gives the minister authority to appoint.
A commissioner or commissioners to in vestigate and report upon the state and management of the business, or any part of tht business, of such department, either in the inside or outside service thereof, and the conduct of any person in such service, so far as relates to his official duties.
That is what the minister has done. The broadest and most complete powers are conferred by this order in council and this statute upon Mr. Justice Cassels. If these gentlemen have anything to say about Mer-win, if these hon. gentlemen have anything to say about the ' Arctic,' if these hon. gentlemen have anything to say about any of these stories that they have been circulating up and down this country, this gives to Mr. Justice Cassels full and complete authority to investigate and to put on record before this House and the country his findings and report so that this House and the people may deal, not with the insinuations and innuendoes that have been hurled up and down through the country by hon. gentlemen who have abandoned every shred of policy upon every question and who have got down to that one and only occupation as a political party, but with the report and findings of Mr. Justice Cassels. We will have an investigation upon all these insinuations under this statute and order in council which will enable us to have the findings and report so that we will understand the truth in regard to this matter. This inquiry is limited, is it ?
The commissioner or commissioners may, for the purposes of the investigation, enter into and remain within any public office or institution, and shall have access to every part thereof, and may examine all papers, documents, vouchers, records and books of every kind belonging thereto, and may summon before him or them any person and require him to give evidence on oath, orally or in writing, or on solemn affirmation if he is entitled to affirm in civil matters; and any such commissioner may administer such oath or affirmation.
It gives him the fullest and most complete power In order that, if there has been wrongful dealing in regard to supplies, in order, if the officials of the department, not within the last year or two but at any time in the past, have been serving two masters he can find it out. So, it will be with reference to the whole catalogue and category of insinuations that we have heard upon this matter. This inquiry is not restricted. This inquiry goes to the very widest limit in order that there may be a most complete report in regard to anything that may be deemed to be wrong in the Department of Marine and Fisheries. So much for the question as to whether this inquiry is restricted. Some hon. gentlemen have suggested that if there were such and such a thing it would not be possible to investigate it. I am sure that my hon. friends who make this suggestion are dealing in casuistry. Does any one suppose that Mr. ^Justice Cassels, if he found, in any of these things, a suggestion of partnership on the part of any official or minister with anybody dealing with the department, disclosed upon any document which he has the right to scrutinize to the fullest possible extent and limit, would not report to this House and put on record before the House and the country what the facts may be in regard to the matter? I think it is not fair for hon. gentlemen to attempt to suggest that there Is a restricted inquiry here. They feel their weakness on this subject because we have tacked on to this the weakest kind of an argument that could possibly be made

in regard to a subject of this kind. Now, one hon. gentleman lauds Mr. Justice Cas-sels at one moment and another hon. gentleman suggests that if the government had chosen the old Civil Service Commissioners to conduct this investigation it would have been far better. If Mr. Justice Cassels is the good, the upright and the honourable judge, if he is half as worthy as hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House tell us he is he is surely qualified to make this investigation. But, these hon. gentlemen tell us in one breath that he is an upright and honourable judge and in the next breath they tell us that he is not the man for the place. But, if he is half as worthy as hon. gentlemen on the other side contend he is
Who said he was not the man for the place?

Surely the hon. gentleman (Mr. Ward) could not have been in the House or he would have heard the hon. member beside him (Mr. Northrup) suggesting that it was an indication that the government did not want to get at the truth because if they did they would have left the matter to the old commission.
I raised no point as to the integrity of Mr. Justice Cassels.

I criticised the government for appointing Mr. Justice Cassels to conduct such a limited inquiry.

My hon. friend has been too long at the bar and has had too much experience not to know that if Mr. Justice Cassels is half as good a man as my hon. friend says he is he will, with the powers which he has under this statute and under this order in council, be able to investigate anything that my hon. friend has ever insinuated against the department during the past five or six years.
He will be hauled over the coals for going beyond his powers. The commissioners have been blamed for doing that.

Well, I can assure my hon. friend that there is not the Mr. MACDONALD.
slightest evidence of any restriction of the inquiry in this case. It is impossible for them to argue that there is. They have taken the position at one moment of saying that Mr. Cassels is a very able man and at the next moment declaring that this investigation would have been very much better conducted if it had been conducted by the Civil Service Commissioners. And then, as if they knew precisely the untenable position they were in they take the other course: they are driven to the weakest possible position, they turn around and abuse the counsel who have been called in by the government to take part in this investigation. Of course the old game is to abuse the lawyer on the other side, and my hon. friends opposite have got themselves into the very weakest possible position when they say that though these are able men, yet they are Liberals and all kind of things must be suspected about them. I apprehend that the record of the Hon. Mr. Justice Cassels at the bar and the estimation in which he is held by all who know him must be kpown to these gentlemen opposite, and if Mr. Justice Cassels is to carry our his powers under the statute and under the order in council, it is a most unwarranted assumption that men of the standard of Mr. Watson and Mr. Perron would be found disregarding their oath not merely as barristers but as King's Counsellers, to endeavour to prevent Mr. Justice Cassels from conducting a proper investigation. I submit that when these gentlemen read the report of the Civil Service Commission they will find that the clause which is contained in this order in council is the only portion of the report which makes any imputation on that

department in the sense in which an investigation should be held. I submit that the statute and the order in council give the fullest possible powers to deal with the question, and as to the rest of the arguments of liou. gentlemen opposite they are unwarranted and unfair, and snch arguments would not be advanced if these gentlemen were at the bar discussing this question or anywhere else than in this House where they seem to constantly prostitute almost every public question for partisan ends.

We have had the pleasure of hearing the same stero-typed address from my hon. friend from Pictou when he rises so often in defence of everything wrong that is done by the present government of which he is such an ardent supporter. In the Public Accounts Committee when we endeavour to discover the wrong-doings of the government the hon. gentleman leads the forces in defence of every act of the government and we are therefore not surprised that to-night he should come to their rescue in this matter. Bet me in the first place direct the attention of the Minister of Finance to a statement made by him this afternoon, that the Liberal Conservative party appointed a royal commission to investigate the civil service in 1S91, and that when the report of that royal commission was presented to the House in 1892 the Liberal Conservative party pigeon-holed that report. I take up the * Hansard ' for 1893 and I find that the Liberal Conservative government introduced a Bill for the purpose of bettering the civil service and carrying out in some respects the recommendations of the royal commission. And Sir, we find the Reform party then in opposition condemning the Liberal Conservative government of the day for proposing to make changes in the Civil Service Act, and among the chief of those who objected was Mr. Laurier, now the Prime Minister of Canada. At page 2815 ' Hansard ' 1893. Mr. Laurier said :
The hon. gentleman's demand is not logical. If I agree to the principle of the Bill, 1 would give every facility to perfect it, but we object to the Bill in toto and object that it should go any further.
In the discussion Mr. Laurier said :
I look upon the Bill as a device to put pensioners upon the civil list, and there is no other reason for it. I therefore move that the Bill be not now read a second time but that it be read a second time this day six months.
Here we have it that when the Liberal Conservative government was making an effort to reform the civil service and carry out some of the provisions of the commissioners' report, Mr. Laurier moved the six months hoist. And in face of that the Minister of Finance stands up to-day and states that the Liberal Conservative party
did nothing to carry out the recommendations.

That is not what you said.

Was that a fair statement of the efforts of the Conservative party to improve the civil service.

Yes, we have the Liberal party driven out of power in the province of Ontario for the next twenty-five years.
Huron for instance.
What about Colchester?
My hon. friend need not worry about Huron.
It suits me first-rate.

It is strange these hon. gentlemen opposite are always referring to the Liberal-Conservative party. The government have appointed a commission to look

into some of the departments ; this commission has made a report such as was never presented to any other government in the history of this country ; and we have now the spectacle of one minister after another condemning the three commissioners. What the Liberal-Conservative party say is that after the government have appointed three commissioners to investigate the civil service and the question of civil service reform, and after the commissioners have at considerable expense travelled to different parts of the country, taken many pages of evidence, given their best attention to the question, and made a report, if there are to be any further suggestions, they should come from these three gentlemen, instead of another man being appointed to look into the matter. As to whether or not Mr. Justice Cassels is the proper man to make the investigation I have nothing to say. In any city in Canada you can find men qualified for such a duty. I will wait until Mr. Justice Cassels brings in a report, and I will judge from that whether he is the proper man or not.
The Minister of Justice twitted the Liberal-Conservative party with the statement that the Ontario government had appointed commissioners to look into various matters in the province of Ontario, and I am sure that the hon. Minister of Justice did not do any credit to the position he holds in this government when he said that these commissioners were political heelers. Mr. Whitney's government did appoint some commissions, and the men who composed those commissions were respectable gentlemen, eminently qualified to discharge their duties, and they brought in some reports that were rather damaging to the Reform government in the province of Ontario and the Reform party in Canada. I may point out that one commission they appointed was the School book Commission. My hon. friend the Minister of Railways will know something about that, because he voted in the Ontario legislature that the school-books were supplied to the children of the province of Ontario at the proper price ; and when the Liberal-Conservative party introduced a resolution to the effect that the price was altogether too high, my hon. friend supported a motion that the prices were all right. When the Liberal-Conservative party came into power, Mr. Whitney's government did appoint a commission to inquire into the school-book question : and what did that commission find ? They found that the children were paying twice as much for their school-books as they should, and reported accordingly. Here is an object lesson for my hon. friend, if he is seeking one. When that commission reported, Mr. Whitney set about to take some advantage of the report, with the result that to-day the children of the province of Ontario are paying Mr. BLAIN.
for their school-books less than half of what they did when the Reform party was in power.
One would suppose from this discussion that there was nothing wrong in any department except the Department of Marine and Fisheries ; but all that one has to do is to turn up almost any page of the commission's report to learn the contrary. For instance, my hon. friend the Minister of Customs thinks his department is all right. Let me read a paragraph at page 29 of the report, which says :
Every collector of customs has been appointed from the ranks of the party in power at the moment. Many of the inspectors are in a similar position, and, under a clause of the Civil Service Act waiving the examination of persons appointed to positions requiring special and technical qualifications, almost all the appraisers in the outside service of this department have been appointed without undergoing the Civil Service examination.
When we say anything about men appointed to positions in the Customs Department, the minister's answer always is that they must pass the civil service examination ; and yet the commission reports that a large number of the men appointed by my hon. friend have not passed any such examination. Then, we have a comparatively new minister in charge of the Post Office Department, and I would like to draw his attention to what is said at page 31 of the report :
Tour commissioners found that in all the post office branches officials were employed who had failed to pass the examination laid down by the Act.
These hon. gentlemen came into office with the promise to the people of Canada that they would purify the civil service ; and when we charged that they were appointing political supporters regardless of their qualifications, we were met with the statement that they would be required to pass the civil service examination, and yet we find these commissioners saying that in the Department of Customs and in the Post Office Department officials have been appointed who did not pass any civil service examination whatever. Then, we have a new condition of things. According to this report, not only <lo the politicians who support the present administration use their influence to have men appointed to office, but they use their influence to have the same men promoted. At page 27 of the report the commissioners say : '
As a rule your commissioners found in the outside service that politics enter into every appointment, and politicians on the spot _ interest themselves not only in the appointments but in subsequent promotions of officials.
I do not, Mr. Speaker, wish to detain the House longer. I wish only to say that in

my humble opinion w:hen an inquiry is commenced, and when men have been selected to make that inquiry, and they have done their duty up to a certain point, if there is a necessity for further investigation, it should be referred back to the same men to do that work ; and I am very much surprised that after the government appointed three gentlemen with special qualifications to deal with this matter, and after these gentlemen have brought in a report dealing with different departments of this government and stating that they have found some men making an attempt to serve two masters, we have the government appointing another commission to find out which of these masters these officials are serving.
Surely the men who are appointed to do that, who after examination found that such a condition of things existed, were better qualified than any other men to put then- finger upon the men who are making an effort to serve two masters, which cannot be successfully done. I agree with the proposition of the leader of the opposition (Air. R. L. Borden) that the people of this country will not be satisfied. 1 think the mutual praise policy on the part of the Minister of Justice about his old companions in his happy days, that have gone by, in the province of Ontario should cease. When he knew that these men had been engaged in politics and election trials in the past, he should have attached some dignity to his office, if he had no dignity to attach to himself and have said that when a grave question of this kind presents itself to the people of Canada, he would not leave himself open to the suspicion that he appointed a political supporter of his to defend the government. As the hon. member for Bast Hastings (Mr. Northrup) has pointed out, he could have found honourable men in the profession in any city in Canada, who had no political bias, and I am sure if such men had been found the appointments would not be open to the same objection, and would not receive the same criticism.

Just a few words as my name has been mentioned. I did not intend to take any part in this discussion, but really I have been somewhat struck with the contradictory nature of the arguments, if you may call them so, of the hon. gentlemen opposite. I am trying to see where we are at in this matter. One fault that is found with the appointment of Mr. Justice Cassels is that it is an attempt to review the work of the commissioners, which they say is a highly reprehensible thing to do. Another hon. member says he has not been appointed to review the work of the commissioners at all, only to review one little thing in their report, which is so small that the hon. member for East Hastings wonders that the judge would so lower
himself as to come down from the bench and deal with it.
Another thing that struck me as very remarkable is the attitude of gentlemen belonging to the legal profession. I am but a layman, and have been rather inclined on looking to them as a body of honourable men, men who, if they had a duty placed on them, would discharge it honestly. But if I am to take what I have heard from the member from Toronto, the member from Simcoe and the member from East Hastings, who belong to that great profession, their idea of the sense of honour that dwells in some of their number, is apparently such that one is tempted to ask if they could trust themselves in an investigation of this kind. Could my hon. friend have confidence in himself if he was appointed on a Whitney commission ? Surely he could, at least I think he could, although he has shaken my faith. The other gentlemen who have spoken, every one of them belonging to that profession, have taken the ground that men sworn to do their duty, sworn in a judicial investigation, will disregard their obligation. It is not my judgment.
The hon. member for East Hastings (Mr. Northrup) tells us this is a little, trifling, contemptible task to ask the judge to descend from the bench and undertake. In the same breath he tells us that this judge is a noble man. He must be that, for he has always had the admiration of my hon'. friend, and that would prove him to be a noble man. This noble man so misapprehends the nature of the duties he has been asked to perform that he is not able to see, what the profound brain of the hon. member for East Hastings could see, that the inquiry is a little, miserable, contemptible thing that he should not have taken hold of. He was not compelled to do so. The government recommended him for appointment and he accepted the appointment. Why on earth did he do it ? Why could he not have some conception of the dignity of his office equal to that of the member for East Hastings (Mr. Northrup). Why could he not have asked him, why has the hon. member, who loves him so, allowed him to accept it ? Why did he not go to him with that lifelong friendship and admiration and say : Judge, you will never think of taking that, surely ? Why it is the meanest, smallest, most contemptible task ever given to a man 1 He did not do it, he has let the poor judge get into that scrape. Think of it! He assures us that he took care to laud the judge to the highest point. So do they all, the member for Toronto, the member for Simcoe, they all upheld him in that.
These hon. members have their own appreciation of what members of the profession, sworn to perform a judicial act, will do. How do they know what they will

do ? Is it a common thing in the profession, has it been known in the profession that members act in that way ? If I should take that low estimate of these men, which I utterly repudiate, let us see how this admiration for the honour and ability of the hon. judge comes in. Surely, with his ability and his honour, if he found these gentlemen who are chosen to assist him in his duty, which is to arrive at facts, not to prosecute anybody, trying to hide the facts, trying to pervert the work they have undertaken to do, and if he allowed them to do so, he would not be of the character given him by the hon. members for Bast Simeoe, East Hastings and Toronto. They cannot take that position. You can see at once, Mr. Speaker, how bewildered I have been with the arguments of the hon. gentlemen opposite. Such a thing could not happen or Judge Cassels cannot be the man these gentlemen say he is. If he allowed that to take place he would lack either discernment, capacity or honesty, and they dare not charge him with such a lack. Is my argument good or not ?
He is appointed to do something which he does not consider beneath his dignity. It is true he is not asked to review the report of the commissioners. The government and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries are willing that this report of the commissioners shall go out, 10,000 copies of it, wherever the members choose to send it. They have the benefit of whatever weight it carries. We do not ask to have it reviewed, we do not ask to have the opinions in it qualified. We do not ask a commission to be appointed to see that if they cannot contradict what has already been reported. That is going out with all the condemnation that it will carry.
Ten thousand copies?
That is the number ordered to be printed, I think.
Two thousand copies.

It is immaterial. It is going out by thousands of copies. And this commission is not appointed to refute or contradict what they have said. But here is the statement of the commissioners that they believe that certain officials in that department are dishonest and corrupt. They do not give the names of these men, and this judicial Inquiry is to ascertain whether there be such men in the service that they may be dealt with. And the investigator will report. We are asked : Why not have called upon the commissioners to do this? Well, I suppose the judge will be at perfect liberty-and for all I know he will do it-to ask the commission to give him the facts. He may say : Here is a charge you have made ; evidently you had reason to believe it is true ; would you please tell me the officers whom you suspect, or refer me to the files of the'de-Mr. PATERSON.
partment that I may trace up the matter tor myself? That is the point we wish to ascertain. Now, this is the one point in this report with which the minister could not deal. He wanted a judicial inquiry, and he is having it. The rest of the report, referring to the correspondence, the duplication of work, the lack of supervision and other weaknesses alleged are departmental in their nature and must be dealt with by the head of the department. And the minister is proceeding to deal with them- started long ago. He has examined into the working of his department, and he is examining into it to see where improvements can be made. The testimony of these commissioners themselves shows that. They say :
There is not only a lack of efficient organization and method in the department. There would also seem to be a lack of conscience.
That is the subject of this investigation. But they say also :
The lack of organization and of organizing power ill. the department has recently been verv conspicuously and painfully illustrated by the fact that the accountant's or bookkeeping branch had apparently fallen into such confusion that expert accountants had to be called in to put things to rights and create some intelligible system. After months of work

So the minister was at this months ago, according to these commissioners.
After months of work by these highly paid experts the result has been at least greatly improved books as far as mechanical form is concerned, but probably little else; and this achievement has been accomplished at an almost fabulous expense.
Oh, oh.
That is in print and it is going out in these 7,000 or 10,000 copies. People will see, at any rate, that action was taken by the minister months before these gentlemen saw his department at all.

Will the hon. gentleman (Mr. Paterson) allow me to ask a question? He has repeated his statement about ten thousand and seven thousand copies going out. Each member receives seven or eight copies, making two thousand in all. What becomes of the rest?

I am speaking merely from memory and am willing to be corrected if I am wrong. Tell me the number.
Mi-. LENNOX. Two thousand.
Can we have the ten thousand ?
I do not know anything about it; that is a matter for the Printing Committee. It is going out in thousands at any rate. There is no attempt to hide it, is there?
I don't know.

It has been in the papers. At any rate, it is shown that the minister, months before these men saw his department, had recognized the weakness of the system and had engaged professional and expert accountants to inaugurate a new system of bookkeeping by which he will be able to check purchases made through the outside agencies of the department. That system these commissioners report to be a great advantage mechanically, but probably little more. I will not stop to ask whether that was a well considered or a fair expression on the part of the commissioners, for I am not here to criticise them. But if one were criticising he might ask how these men could know that the system was of little use, for that was a matter to be determined in the future and by experience. The minister was carrying on his reorganization. What does these hon. gentlemen opposite want? I would like to ask the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Poster), if he were in his place, or the hon. member for South Lanark (Mr. Haggart), they being the only two gentlemen who have had the responsibility of administering a department, what either of them would have done if he had been at the head of a department and a report of this kind had been made? To hear hon. gentlemen opposite talk one would suppose that it was the duty of these commissioners to go into the Department of Marine and Fisheries, turn the minister out of doors and reorganize the business themselves. They did their duty when they pointed out what seemed to them weakness in the department-just as they did in my department. I have no fault to find with them for pointing out these weaknesses, for if there is anyone interested in knowing the facts concerning the management of the department it is the minister in charge. A minister values his reputation as hon. gentlemen opposite value theirs. If he has any ability he wants to exercise it and wants to get due credit for exercising it and for doing the best he can. What could these commissioners do except to point out where they thought weaknesses existed? The Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Brodeur) will not object to that. He will look through their recommendations and if he agrees that there are weaknesses he will strengthen the department at those points. That is what I would do in my department.
They did not come into my department, the inside. They asked the commissioner if Mr. Bazin and Mr. Fyshe would be allowed to come in. Why, he said, most certainly. And so they would. I would be glad to have them go through, and if they found any weakness, if they could suggest any better way of managing anything in my department, and my judgment agreed with theirs, I would adopt it. I may be egotistical, but I believe that I can run my department better than they can. I am not going to say that I would neglect any good suggestions they might make to me. I would examine their suggestions. I would test them, but I would not adopt them if they did not commend themselves to my judgment-not if I were a free agent. Even though these gentlemen should go cursorily through my department and think they saw on the surface some weak point which they thought could be remedied, I would listen to their suggestions, and I would accept them if I thought they were an improvement. If they found that some of the work was being duplicated in the Marine Department, if they found that some of the officers had not carried out their instructions, why, I have no doubt that my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Brodeur) would see what he could do to improve matters. He started in to do this months ago, and he is at it now. and he will accomplish it.
