I say to hon. gentlemen opposite that in all fairness they had better wait and see in what shape he gets his department, wait and see What the report of Judge Cassels is. The hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain) says he is going to wait, he is not going to pronounce judgment until he sees the report of Judge Cassels. He is a wiser and more prudent man that the hon. member for Hastings (Mr. Northrup) and some other gentlemen who are willing to judge the minister before they see the report. It would not be the part of wisdom for the minister to sit in a judicial capacity on these men in his department who are charged with being corrupt and dishonest; he asks for the assistance of a judge to look into the facts, and he gets that assistance. When the report is made it will be his duty to examine it and see if there are any suggestions in it that will improve present conditions, and if he finds any that commend themselves to his judgment, I have no doubt that he will give effect to them. Hon. gentlemen opposite have taken two lines of argument. First they object to this commission because they say it is going to review the work of the previous commissioners and upset it. Nothing of the kind. There are two specific instances which the commissioners give as acts of maladministration, namely in the purchase of coal and in the purchase of flour, but they did not follow their inquiry far enough to learn the facts of the case. But they put these two charges in their report, and that report goes out wherever this volume goes. The commissioners also make a statement with reference to my department, I do not speak of this with any idea of weakening their statement, but only to point out that in the short time at their disposal they were not able to get at the real facts of the case and to explain the situation fully and fairly to the people. The hon. member for Peel read

something that they said about my department in the outside service. He read this:
Many of the inspectors are in a similar position, and under a clause in the Civil Service Act waiving the examination of persons appointed to positions requiring special and technical qualifications, almost all the appraisers in the outside service of this department have been appointed without undergoing the civil service examination.
Yes, that is true I believe, in some cases it is, and I have never been able to see yet that a man passing the civil service examination was thereby a better appraiser than one who had not passed it.
Will the hon. gentleman read the balance of that section ?

I am coming to that I think it was a collector of customs at Quebec that they were questioning, and I think he said that according to his recollection one man had been plucked because he did not know who the Druids were. He could not get through. Now I do not care whether an appraiser knows who the Druids were or not, but I want him to know whether goods are linen or cotton, or something else. In our department we need to appoint men who understand their business, and all the collegiate institutes or university training in the world will not make a man a good appraiser if he knows nothing about the quality of goods. But no man has been appointed appraiser without undergoing the technical examination which is prescribed in the Act and which is given ]him Iby a superior officer. If he passes that successively he is recommended to me by the commission.
Were there any cases of men who were plucked?
There may have been some cases where applicants to appraiser-ships were plucked because they were not sufficiently conversant with their business.

The commissioners complain that my hon. friend appoints appraisers who do not pass the civil service examination. My hon. friend says they do not require to pass it, but he has a special examination for them. Now when one of his supporters in the House recommends to him a man for an appraiser, has any one of these men been rejected because he could not pass the special examination he refers to ?

I cannot remember. But if none of them were rejected, it would show the discernment of our supporters in the House. But I only want to tell the hon. gentleman that he is not appointed on the recommendation of a member of the House unless he passes a practical examination. That is what we start with.

Although the commissioners condemn that policy of appointment Mr. PATERSON.
without passing the civil service examination my hon. friend is not going to pay any attention to their recommendation ?

Their judgment and mine do not run in the same direction. Passing the civil service examination would not hurt a man. It is a literary examination. Who were the Druids ? What happened in King Charles time ? and so oh. It would not hurt a man provided he had the technical knowledge as well, but to require a man to pass the civil service examination alone, which is purely literary and to accept him as an appraiser on that is not, I think my hon. friend will agree, the wisest thing to do.	-
What I say is that when we have the civil service examination my hon. friend should either apply it to the officers of his department or else.abolish the examination altogether.
That is not necessary, because a part of the Civil Service Act expressly states that in the case of technical officers the civil service literary examination may be dispensed with.
Make it easy for political purposes.

No, no ; that is the Act. Now, the hon. gentleman asks me to read a little farther :
In the service of this department

That is In reference to the Customs Department-
-there are many anomalies and incongruities. In order to avoid the necessity of an examination a new class has been created under the name of ' examining officers/ a class not found in the schedule to the Civil Service Act.
Is that the point that my hon. friend wanted me to read ?
Yes:

I am very glad he did. I ask the attention of the House to that especially as my hon. friend has called attention to it. It is a little valuable because it shows the care that was exercised by these gentlemen. There is a direct statement that :
In order to avoid the necessity of examinations a new class has been created under the name of 'examining officers/ a class not found in the schedule to the Civil Service Act.
Well let us see. Section 39 of the Civil Seivice Act reads as follows :
Notwithstanding anvthing in this Aot a person who has served over three years as an officer or acting officer in the outside service of the customs may be appointed an examining officer in such service subject to such examination on the 'duties of office and other qualifications as is prescribed by the

deputy head in a report to be concurred in by the head of the department.
There it is. This commission say it is not to be found in the schedule of the Act.
Is it found in the schedule to the Act ?

Yes, look at page 20, Schedule. First there are the 'higher classes,' next * technical officers,' next ' other classes ' such as ' examining officers (including lockers and landing waiters) ' with salaries from $400 to $1,000. That is going out in all these thousands of copies all over the country. It is going out to say that in order to avoid examination I have created a new class under the name of examining officers.
That is your royal commission ?
Yes.
Appointed by the government.

I was not finding fault with it. I do wonder, however, that they should have overlooked the Act and not only overlooked the Act but should have put in the report a statement which, as you can see for yourself, is absolutely the reverse of what is in the Act. It is charged that I adopted this new class in order to avoid examination. You gentleman are guilty with me in this matter. A few years ago I was impressed with the fact that we had in the service scores and scores of men, some of whom had been appointed twenty-five years, some eighteen years, some fifteen years, some twelve years, and some later, under ourselves, although the great bulk of them had been appointed by my predecessors who were, to all intents and purposes, permanent officers. Year in and year out they were there. They were paid year after year, but they were not on the permanent staff, and, not being on the perma-staff, they were not entitled to their three weeks holidays a year and it, unfortunately, they became sick, the department had no power under the law to allow them their salary or to pay their wages ; whereas, if they had been on the permanent list they would have enjoyed the same treatment as that which those on the permanent list enjoy. Many and many-scores-I am not speaking extravagantly - of these men, faithful men, who had been there for years and years, and who were appointed in the days of my hon. friends opposite, were unable to pass the literary examination. I do not know whether I could pass it myself or not. I could have done so when I came out of school, no doubt. I question now whether it would not bother some of you to answer all the questions that are put. A number of these men who had been there for years and years could not hope to pass
this examination. Men who had given faithful service for years and years, 1 thought, were entitled to fair treatment. I introduced into this House a Bill to amend the Civil Service Act in order to enable that to be done. These hon. gentlemen opposite as well as gentlemen on this side of the House endorsed that Bill. They were parties to it. I hold it was right. I glory that I did it. Many of these men, faithful servants, serving as faithfully as any man who had passed the civil service literary examination, which is all that is required under the Act, were in the position that I have described. Instead of, as the commissioners say, appointing that class with the view of avoiding examination it is provided that when they have been three years or more in the service you can prescribe a practical examination for them in the duties of the office they are discharging and if they pass that successfully-and what more do you want-then, on my recommendation, they are put on the permanent list, the men's hearts and the hearts of their wifes and families are made glad and justice is done to them and the country. Was it to avoid examination ? No, it was not that they could be put on as preventive officers without any examination at all, but it was because I wanted them to undergo an examination in the duties of their office. What surprises me is that it escaped the attention of the chairman of this commission when such a sentence as this was put in their report.
He was secretary of the treasury board for a considerable time after this was inaugurated and the way the special examinations take place is this :	The officer applies for an examination, the commissioner prescribes the examination and I don't see it, it is sent to a superior officer who is generally the inspector of the . division, the officer undergoes the examination and if he is successful the inspector reports to the commissioner and the commissioner reports to me and recommends that the appointment be conferred, and that report passes through the hands of the secretary of the treasury board, and a number of such reports must have passed through Mr. Courtney's hands. How such a sentence could be inserted there baffles me and leads me to think that some one who did not understand the thing is a party to it and not Mr. Courtney. Is my hon. friend from Peel satisfied I have read that now. Now, Mr. Speaker, I believe that what the government have done in this matter will find justification in the country. While I recognize the right of the opposition to get all the advantage they possibly can in a fair and legitimate way, yet there is such a thing as pursuing certain tactics too far. I ask these gentlemen opposite : Have they in any degree whatever given fair play to that man who only came into his office two years ago and who of neces-

sity lias been absent from it for months and months together, and especially when that very report states that months and months ago he started to get the department into better shape. Appoint your commission again if you want it to go through my department. I will welcome it and so would the Minister of Marine and Fisheries welcome it, but we would like them to go to the bottom of things and when they do report to be sure that they report facts, especially when their report is to go broadcast over the country.
What objection can the hon. gentleman have to referring the report back to these three gentlemen.

They finished their work. The government did not call them off. It was their duty to do that work and if they felt unwilling or unable to do it surely that is enough. We accept their work except where they make that insinuation or implied charge against the honesty of the officials of that department and we inquire into that. No man is more interested in having his department right than the minister in charge. And when these gentlemen opposite say the people of Canada will not be satisfied with our action, the true fact is that what they want is that the people of the country should not be satisfied. Did not the member for Beau-harnois tel] us that it means party advantage and gain to them, and how dear that is to their souls, their speeches of this afternoon show when they did not hesitate to insinuate against the honour of men of their own profession, and against the character either because of weakness or incapacity of an honourable judge who stands amongst the highest in the community.

I shall not detain the House long, but it would not be right to allow some of the observations of the Minister of Customs to pass unchallenged. The hon. gentleman said that the hon. member for Hastings complained that Judge Cassels should undertake such a limited task, and yet in the same breath declared him to be an upright, capable and honourable judge. No oue ou this side of the House refutes that. AVe do not complain of the character of the man but we do complain that the order of reference is so circumscribed that Judge Cassels can only deal with a small fraction of what in the interests of the country he should deal with. Did not the Minister of Justice complain that the old commission went outside of their order of reform ? Did he not cite two iustauces to prove this and did he not state that the allegations they made were not founded on fact. Then the Minister of Marine and Fisheries states that with regard to certain things in his department the allegations in that report are absolutely incorrect. When the Minister of Marine and Fisheries presented that report to the House Mr. PATERSON
he stated that some of the allegations in the report were wrong, and the Minister of Justice and the Minister of Customs endorse that statement, and they say another commission must be appointed presumably for the purpose of determining whether the allegations made by the first commission are right or wrong. This shows, Sir, that it is the Civil Service Commission that is on trial and not the department, and that is one of the reasons why the government were afraid to reappoint the same commissioners and allow them to finish the work which they declared they had not time to finish. The Minister of Justice stated that the leader of the opposition asked the government to appoint a Committee of the House or an independent commission, and that in appointing Judge Cassels they had followed the advice of the leader of the opposition. That statement is not correct. What the leader of the opposition said was that because the old commission had not inquired into one quarter of the things it should in the interests of the country have inquired into, and had only dealt in a perfunctory way with one or two departments, the matter should be referred either to a Committee of the House or to an independent commission to go through all the departments and to finish the work which the commission had only commenced. Has the government appointed Judge Cassels to completejhe work which the Civil Service Commission left off ? Not at all. They appointed a commissioner but thev limited the work of that commissioner and restricted him to an inquiry into one allegation against the Marine Department. That is not what the leader of the opposition suggested. Was the hon. leader of the opposition justified in saying that we required another commission ? If you take up the report of the commissioners you cannot reach any other conclusion. What did that report say ?
Large amounts have been spent at several places in the Dominion for supplies bought from those enjoying political patronage at what may be called retail rates. Heavy expenditures have been incurred without necessary consideration or supervision, and while no doubt the several officers have thought themselves justified, owing to the expansion of the revenues, vet such conduct is contrary to the public interests and. in the opinion of the commissioners, ought to be restrained.
That applies to any department, and therefore the leader of the opposition said that we wanted another commission to inquire into that subject. Then, the commissioners take up the question of certificates which are made to the effect that tlie goods were required for the public services and that the prices were reasonable and fair. On this point the commissioners say :
In the first place there is the question of certificates. These certificates are in general terms, that the articles have been received,

that the articles are necessary in the public interests, that the prices charged are according to contract, or that the prices are fair and just. In reference to the question of certificates, the Auditor General in his evidence pointed out that in one department he did not believe in the certificates received. This is a very serious affair.
The Auditor General did not regard the certificates as correct or reliable. Is this new commission to inquire into this subject ? Not at all; it is not in the order of reference. Then the commissioners say in regard to the Department of Railways :
Your commissioners are of opinion that in many instances stores are ordered unnecessarily, and it may be doubtful that a good quality is always delivered. Mr. Pottinger states in his evidence that it is his opinion that the amount paid by the Intercolonial Railway for coal was higher than it ought to be. In instances which have been brought to the notice of the commissioners stores have been received which were not wanted and which it is difficult to get rid of. In fact, at different points stores have been shelved where in all probability they were unnecessary.
Will the new commission inquire into that or touch the Intercolonial Railway ? Not at all. That is why we complain- because it has no power to inquire into these matters, which we think ought to be inquired into. I take another department, the Marine and Fisheries Department, as to which the commissioners report :
Your commissioners have spent a _ large amount of time in trying to get an insight into the general administration of the government business, as shown in the management 0f this department. They found that to make any efficient inspection was a matter of enormous difficulty.
Therefore they could Dot make the inspection they desired. Again they say :
There are officers enough in the department, both inside and outside, to do all the work efficiently, if they were properly trained and organized, but there is no efficient organization.
Who is responsible for the efficiency of the organization ? Is it not the head of the department ? Then the report goes on to say :
It is practically impossible to fix the responsibility on anybody. . . There is no sign visible of a single directing head, or an intelligent purpose, unless it be that of spending as much money as possible. . . The lack of organization and of organizing power in the department has recently been very conspicuously and painfully illustrated. . . . There is not only a lack of efficient organization and method in the department. There would also seem to be a lack of conscience.
This new commission is not empowered to make inquiries into the various ramifications of thpt department. It is empowered only to inquire into the allegations made in the order of reference, which applies only to a few sentences of the report. The commissioners say further :
The extracts from the ' challenged accounts ' file show constant inquiries from the Auditor General as to prices, hut there is always some more or less satisfactory explanation, ending with whatever certificates may be necessary, and further investigation baulked.
And yet this new commission is not to go into that inquiry. Are we not justified in saying that it ought to be given wider powers? We are not objecting to the commissioner who is appointed to do the work, if he is only given the power necessary to enable him to go over the whole field. The commissioners say further :
A new officer was appointed in connection with it called the commissioner of lights, whose whole time is now given to its management although it includes the management of a lighthouse depot established at Prescott, where a great variety of work is carried on connected with the lighthouse and buoy service. Your commissioners have to report that in their commission this new departure has been a most unfortunate one so far as the efficiency of the special work is concerned; and it certainly has not added to the general efficiency of the Marine and Fisheries Department.
They follow that up by saying :
There can be very little question that the Lighthouse Board has been the means of greatly increasing the expenditure of the department, and that much of the increase has been wasted.
Yet the new commissioner has no power to inquire into that. The commissioners follow that up by saying :
They have been able to go over only a very small section of even the Marine and Fisheries Department.
To do the work completely, that whole department should be gone over, and the new commissioner has no power to do that work.
Your commissioners have to confess that the general conclusions which they have formed regarding the administration of the department are most unfavourable. It seems to have few redeeming features.
Yet the head of that department is the one responsible for the organization ; but the Dew commission has no power to inquire into that subject. It is because of this that we complain of the limited power given to Judge Cassels. The Minister of Justice argued that the other commissioners went outside of their order of reference ; and if the new commissioner went outside of his order of reference a similar complaint would be made against him. If there is one thing more than another that a



judge or a lawyer always keeps in view, it is that he must he guided by precedent, and all precedent seems to demand that a judge or a commission should keep within the order of reference ; and if they travelled outside of that, the government would condemn them, as the Minister of Justice and the Minister of Customs have condemned the Civil Service Commissioners. And then they have made the order of reference so narrow that he can travel over no field. They have touched on only one or two of the departments. We have many spending departments, we have the Post Office Department, and the great spending Department of Public Works, some transactions of which have been laid bare to the light of day. Even the Marine Department has only been dealt with in a perfunctory way. There is the Interior Department, which administers the lands of the country, the timber limits and immigration. The Militia Department has been barely referred to, and it has been declared that a great deal might be said of it. Then we have the Departments of Agriculture, Customs and Inland Revenue, which are not dealt with in detail. This new commission cannot touch any of these departments except the Department of Marine, and that, only with regard to one or two particular items in the report. It is because of this that complaint is made, and not because of the man who is appointed to do the work. We say there is more to be done and the country will not be satisfied until a full and free inquiry is made in all departments and a report made to the House, so that we will know where it is necessary to make amendments or to reorganize departments in the interest of economy and of honesty. When that is done and not until then, the country will be satisfied that the government have done their full duty in connection with these commissions.

Motion agreed to, and House went into Committee of Supply.
Montreal-barracks for permanent corps,

speakeroldname: Hon. WM. PTJGSLEY (Minister of Public Works).
speechtext: This is a revote to provide towards the erection of barracks for one unit of the permanent corps in Montreal. A request for this building was made by the Department of Militia and it has been urged upon the Public Works Department upon several different occasions. Application was made as early as 1902 and it has been repeated since and the department is strongly of the opinion that this work should be undertaken. The appropriation of 1907-8 was the first vote.
Why was it not commenced ?

There is some land to be acquired by the Militia Department.
Mr. SPROTJLE
The department has made a sale of St. Helen's island to the city of Montreal, for the sum of $200,000 and it is intended by the Militia Department when this money is paid over to appropriate part of it for the purcahse of a site. My information is that Montreal is now about ready to pay over the money and in that case a special appropriation will be asked for in the supplementary estimates to buy the land.

Is this vote conditional on the payment of the $200,000 by the city of Montreal ?
Mr. PUGSLEYr. I cannot say it is conditional. It is not likely that the erection of these barracks will be proceeded with until the money is paid over.

Is it decided where these barracks will be erected ?
Mr. PUGSLEYr. No, I cannot say where they will be.

That is the most important question. Montreal has asked for these barracks for a number of years and I understand the Militia Department have found it impossible to decide on the location. It makes a great difference to the city where it is located. The location may give universal satisfaction or cause general dissatisfaction.

I cannot give the information but my hon. friend will understand that as in the case of a post office an effort will be made to locate it so as to give general satisfaction. The total cost of the building is expected to be $126,000. It is intended to provide quarters for single and married officers, men's barracks, hospital, guard room and cells, recreation room and also-fittings for the buildings.
How much is to be paid for the land?
It is not intended to pay for the land out of this, that will come out of the $200,000.
Is it intended to build the barracks in the Parc Lafontaine ?

There is great objection to having it built in that park. It is one of the few breathing places we have in Montreal and the citizens will object very strongly to having the barracks there. It is hard for the minister to say where it will be. If it is mooted that the land will be purchased in some part of the city, then as my hon. friend who has been in the council and understands land speculation knows, the competition for the sale of land to the department by speculators will be very marked. I do not think it wise now to say where the location will be.
Is it intended to build in the Parc Lafontaine ?
It would be impossible to say that ; I am not informed that the location has been decided on.

The minister has said it would increase the price of land, but the park is the property of the government and that argument would not apply. I know that many citizens object to having it in the park and that is why I want to know if that question has been decided.
I thought I was very frank, I said that I was not informed where the location will be.

With reference to what the Postmaster General (Mr. Lemieux) has said as to keeping this matter secret lest publicity should enhance the price of the property, I think that, perhaps, this side of the House are getting a little tired of that excuse-for we regard it as little better than an excuse. We find it merely a means to facilitate the work of the middleman, who comes in and taxes the people an exorbitant price. Members of the House are aware, that we have expropriation laws which protect the government and the people. When owners demand an exorbitant price, the proper method for the government to follow is to take expropriation proceedings and secure the land at such value as men on their sworn testimony prove to be fair instead of repeating such experiences as we had in Halifax, through Mr. Lodge and others, of being salted for an enormous price for the benefit of a middleman. I for one, take no stock in this excuse that the government is afraid to say that they want a particular property because the price will be put up. We have honest men in the country who will swear to the true value, if the government will make an investigation under the Act and take the property. The person who asks an exorbitant price and does not get it has to pay the costs of the proceedings, and*\ after a few people have had experience of that kind, we shall get land at reasonable prices. Our experience has been that, while the government keeps the information from the House, they give it to one of their friends, on which he goes and gets options and the end is that we pay to this middleman a most exorbitant price.
Can the minister tell us fwhether this building is to be used for artillery, cavalry or infantry, and what number of men it is expected to accommodate?
It is for one unit of the permanent corps.
Which includes

I regret that the minister of Militia (Sir Frederick Borden) is not here. He would be able to give the information. But my hon. friend (Mr. Ames) 2354
will understand that it is rather outside my department.

Can the minister say whether this unit includes cavalry and artillery? That has an important bearing on the situation, because the choice of location should depend a good deal on the nature of the building and how it is to be occupied, If this means keeping a large number of horses in a building in a thickly-peopled part of Montreal, or in a public park, of course that would be a disadvantage. Unless such details are furnished us, we cannot know whether this money should be voted or not.
Would it not be wise to wait until the Minister of Militia is here?
This is only a re-vote.
But the information may not have been out last year, and it is desirable to get it out now.

When the Minister of Militia is here and some other item is under discussion, if any hon. gentleman calls attention to this matter, there will be no objection to the Minister of Militia making an explanation as to the number of men to be accommodated.

With that understanding, it will be all right
Montreal general past office-enlargement additions and alterations, including fittings, furniture, Ac., $70,000.

This is a revote and it is required for the enlarging of the present quarters for the Montreal post office. As many hon. gentlemen are aware, there was an appropriation last session of $300,000. Out of that sum, a property which was owned by the proprietors of the Montreal ' Gazette ' was purchased, and a contract was let for the erection of a building on this site, the contract being for $487,537. In addition to which, of course, there will be other expenditures for heating, fittings, &e.
What will be the total cost?
The total estimated cost, including site is $762,000.
Was it in connection with the new post office that I saw that Mr. Wright had purchased an option?
No, that was in connection with the new examining warehouse.
Who has the contract for building this addition to the post office?
Messrs. Peter Lyall & Son, Montreal. There were several tenders, of which Messrs. Lyall's was the lowest. A day or two ago, in answer to a question, I gave a statement as to the different tenders.
I noticed in the newspapers an account of a banquet in Montreal tendered to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) at which a Mr. Lyall was chairman; is this the same gentleman?
The very same gentleman-and a very excellent citizen of Montreal he is.
This would seem to be only an enlargement of the old post office?

It is more than that. It is the building of an addition. The 'Gazette' property is on the opposite side of Fortification Lane from the post office, and is to be wholly occupied with the addition to the post office, connection to be made across Fortification Lane.
What area of land was purchased?

I have not the figures relating to the land before me, but it will explain the matter as well, perhaps, if I say that the addition is to extend from the present post office building along St. Francois Xavier street to Craig street, 126 feet, and along Craig street 96 feet.
Then, this will be larger than the old building?
I think so.
Does the government need as large a place as that?

Oh, yes. The present post office was built in 1874, and as my hon. friend from St. Antoine (Mr. Ames) knows, is entirely inadequate for the postal service of Montreal. When the translantic mails arrive in Montreal, the condition of the post office is simply chaos. Even the offices of the postmaster and his assistants in Montreal are taken during the Christmas season for the foreign mail. Today we have no place for our employees, and it is a great relief to know that at last we are to have a decent building for our staff. The population is now nearly half a million. With the addition of the new suburbs Montreal is going far ahead of Toronto.
But the revenue of the post office is not as great.

In the statement I gave of the total cost I omitted the cost of acquiring in Montreal the right to utilize Fortification lane. The corporation require us to pay rent the same as they charge the Bank of Montreal. But they also agreed to commute that if we desired, and we decided to commute it into a capital payment I think of $11,000. That should be added to the total cost.

I understood the government are spending some $762,000 in Montreal, and does he mean to say that the cor-Mr. PUGSLEY.
poration are asking the government $11,000 for the right to cross Fortification lane?

The reason is that there is some law of general application, and the city requires us to pay the same as the Bank of Montreal. This building is to have a basement and a bridge 70 by 25 feet thrown over Fortification lane.

The Montreal public have, I think, been long suffering from lack of conveniences in the post office. They have pointed out many times to the Postmaster General that there was great congestion in the old building. I hope the Postmaster General realizes that when this new building is constructed it will be necessary also to reconstruct the entire postal staff as well as the building. I have in my hand a letter which was published in the ' Star ' on the 8th April, signed by a well known lawyer, in which he draws attention to at least five cases where letters have been mailed and have never reached the parties to whom they were addressed. That I presume is largely due to the past state of affairs. We can only hope that when the new building is constructed there will be a complete remodeling, not only of the facilities, but also of the staff.

I must protest on behalf of the employees of the Montreal post office against a too severe criticism. There has been a wonderful improvement within a year or so. In the old days I know there were many complaints, due chiefly to the fact that the salaries were inadequate. I hope the new Civil Service Bill will provide better salaries for our employees. On the other hand, I am pleased to state that we have appointed as assistant postmaster in Montreal, Mr. Gaboury, who has given entire satisfaction to the citizens. The other day I was present at an interview with the members of the produce exchange and of .the board of trade and they highly complimented Mr. Gaboury on the success of his new methods. I am aware of this letter published in the 'Star,' signed by my friend Mr. McCormick. When I heard of the complaints I ordered an investigation. I gather from reports I have that Mr. McCormick might perhaps publish another letter to say that the fault was not in the post office, but in his own office. However, the investigation will prove who was to blame. Within the last eighteen months we have reorganized the letter-carrier service and put it in a very satisfactory shape. I hope if the citizens will be patient a little longer they will have just as good a system of delivery as there is in other large centres. I admit that in the Montreal post office for some years past there has been at work some influence which prevented the staff from doing its duty towards the public. But since the appointment of Mr. Gaboury there has been a marked change for the better.
What influence does the minister refer to?

The old officers had lost all control over the later appointments. We had men there who had been in the service for forty years, and they had no control at all over the employees, for reasons which I need not detail to the House. But since Mr. Gaboury's appointment there has beeD a great improvement.

I would like to know why the people in the country districts should not be as well treated in regard to postal facilities as the people of cities. Why does the government build a post office in one place and refuse to build one in another equally deserving? I know of places with a population of 1,500 to 2,500 and the government will not build a shed for them. I will not speak of Dorchester county, for that has been on the blacklist for a long time. Put take the county of Beauce. The towns of St. Mary, St. Joseph, St. Francois; St. George, Tring, St. Ephraim and like towns have two or three thousand of a population, and yet you will find the post office in a little room eight by ten feet, and a person who goes in before you has to come out before you can get in. There is no accommodation whatever. The government do not even pay rent to the people who keep the post office. Why cannot you do a little more for the rural districts and do a little less for the cities?
The hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) would not agree with that.
I do not ask for a building in my own county. We have not one building erected by the government.

I like to bear my hon. friend talk. He is very sensible and I think his views are very worthy of consideration. His views and mine are alike ; I am a very strong believer in giving accommodation to the public in the way of post office buildings in various sections of the country. Of course, as my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) said last evening, we must go slowly and people must be patient We cannot erect these buildings all at once. We are doing the best we can, we are proceeding with reasonable expedition and as the business of the country will permit.
Some people appear to be welcome aDd others are not.

I wish to say, in reference to the observation of the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Talbot), that the hon. member for East Grey does not agree exactly with him. What was the principle I laid down ? That where the government could not rent a building at a reasonable price they should erect one.
That is just the reverse of the position taken by the hon. member for Dorchester. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) says that instead of building they should rent.
Whenever the government cannot rent a suitable building at a moderate figure they should erect one.
You and the hon. member for Dorchester cannot agree.
The hon. member for Dorchester says that you do not even pay rent for these buildings.

The salary of the postmaster is based on the revenue and on the revenue also is based the rental allowance which is given to every postmaster. A post office which gives a revenue of $10 or $15 is not entitled to a large rental allowance.
There is no rental for a small post office.
Yes.
What rental is there for a post office which gives a revenue of $50 ?
I cannot give it offhand, but I know there is an allowance.
There is no rental at all. It is not always according to the revenue, because no matter what the revenue is the postmaster gets $50. That is according to the Act.

$35 is the minimum. As to the rental allowance, I cannot give the graduation just now, but it is based on the. revenue. I receive every day, letters from all parts of the country asking for increases and I spend my time signing letters explaining that the rental allowance is based on the revenue of the office.

In the county of Montma-gny there was a man who had a house. He could not sell it and he could not give it away. He is a gentleman in the Senate. We must Dot mention his name at all ; his name is Mr. Choquette. Well, he got the Minister of Public Works to buy this building for $4,994.50. As I said last night, two years afterwards, the house fell down. What is the population of the town ? 1,600. When that building went down, they said : We must build one or buy one. These people had to be accommodated because Mr. Choquette lives there sometimes. The county is a Liberal county and no matter what takes place they must be accommodated. Here is the town of Levis with a population of 7,783 and a $49,000 building is being erected. Is there any equality in the treatment of the people in that case ? I will not say anything about Dorchester, but take the county of Beauce. Beauce has a population of 45,000 and there is not

a post office in it belonging to the government. The government have done nothing for the county in that regard. If you do not want to treat Dorchester right you are welcome ; we can get along without you ; we do not ask any favours, but why should you not treat the country on an equality ? It looks-I have said it in the House already and I am going to repeat it, and if the chairman wants to call me to order he may do so-as if the government were in this case, the biggest bribers in the world. Have I not heal'd time and time again members of this House say : I am afraid that I will be defeated in my county in this campaign, I am going to get them a post office or a public building or a railway, and that will help me. Then, they brag that they have got a building, or a wharf or a pier built in their county, and they say that it will help them.
Would the hon. gentleman regard it as a bribe if we were to think it desirable in the public interest to erect a post office in his county ?

Of course if we had to take your word we would do so, but you know very well you are not serious in what you say. If you are, I do not believe you. The government help these men to be elected in their counties. If a man has not the confidence of the people to be returned to this House, he should stay at home. Not very long ago, I heard a member boast that he had 65 miles of railway built in his county, and he would be elected for years to come, and another said his election was sure, because a wharf had been built in his county that cost $10,000 or $12,000. The government bribe people in that way, it may be indirect, but it is bribery all the same. In my county the government never spent a dollar, but we have to pay the bribes for other counties.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Morin) stated yesterday and he has repeated it to-night that Senator Choquette sold a building to the government for a post office and that after it was sold it fell down. Is the hon. member serious in making that statement ?
I will tell you plainly, I don't want you to talk to me and I don't want to talk to you.

I shall not resent that impolite remark of the hon. gentleman but I thought he might address the chair. The statement made by the hon. member with regard to the post office is not correct. In the first place only part of the roof fell down and at the time it fell it was not occupied as a post office. It was only when the whole thing was put in proper shape that the post office was located there.

There was a total expenditure last year of $1,571 for a pneumatic Mr. MORIN.
tube system in Montreal which I understand has been abandoned. That requires some explanation. Then, the Postmaster General referred to the reorganization of the Montreal post office and he spoke of the deputy postmaster as carrying on this reorganization passing over the postmaster who is paid a large salary. Perhaps the postmaster was a political appointee and had no qualification for the office.

Mr. Harwood who was a-respected member of this House for years was appointed postmaster at Montreal, but unfortunately he had to .undergo a severe operation which was the occasion of his ill-health for a year and a half, and on account of which he could not give to his duties the attention which he otherwise would. Fortunately Mr. Harwood has now recovered and is able to discharge his duties in the Montreal post office. He is a very able man and is much respected in the office. When I spoke of the reorganization of the office I referred to Mr. Gaboury, because it is Mr. Gaboury who has special charge of the employees. Mr. Gaboury started from the lowest grade in the service and has attained to his present position through his own merits. Mr. Harwood and he are working hand in hand and I am sure the results of their labours will give satisfaction to the city. As to the pneumatic system, when Sir William Mulock was Postmaster General he intended to introduce that system in Montreal and Toronto. It has proved a success in large cities like London, Liverpool, Berlin, New Yoi'k and Chicago. But in view of the climatic conditions in Montreal and the large expenditure its installation would entail it was thought that for the present the money had better be applied to other more immediate needs in the postal service. Some pipe was purchased for the tube system and that can be sold by the Department of Public Works at any time.
Was land purchased opposite the Bonaventure station for the pneumatic system and is that land still owned by the government.
I think it has been exchanged with the Grand Trunk Railway Company for another lot.
Where is the lot that has been given the government to exchange for the lot opposite the station.
On Imperial avenue.
What use does the government intend to make of the lot on Imperial avenue ?
Why did you not sell the original lot instead of trading it.
It was thought we made a good exchange.
Is this going to be a case of an exchange of a better for a worse article until iinally the money is lost?
I think we made a very fair exchange.

I understand that an extensive set of plans, costing nearly $9,000, were prepared by Mr. Maurice Perreault. These plans, I understand, were paid for by the government. In whose possession are the plans to-day? The city of Montreal had an experience of a similar kind with this gentleman, and he undertook to hold the plans.
The chief architect tells me that the plans are in the department, the property of the department.
If the government decide to construct a system of this character, have they the full right to use these plans?
Certainly. They are the property of the department, and the department can use them at any time.
I understand that the materials purchased for this system are still in the hands of the department, and. will be sold as old junk for whatever they will bring.
We have a certain quantity of pipes in Montreal and also a quantity in Toronto.
What is the value?
I have not the particulars at this moment, as I did not expect this matter to come up under this item.

I think this is rather important. Here we have a government purchasing a large quantity of pipes, purchasing land, getting out plans and spending a large amount of money in connection with a system which they have abandoned altogether. Among the items we find that they are paying $75 a month to a political supporter in Montreal for the storage of the pipes.
We are not paying storage now. We are storing them on our own land.
When did the rental for the storage of pipes cease, and what property was being occupied before by the storage of those pipes?
The charge for storage ceased on the first of the present year, when the pipes were removed to a lot owned by me government, and were stored free of cost in a shed erected for that purpose.
What qualification had this gentleman for making these plans ?
He was an architect.

And he was paid the sum of $9,000 to do what the chief architect at Ottawa, with his twelve assistants, could not do. Is this a part of that $100,Out) which was paid out so generously by this government to the architects of Canada, or is it in addition to that?
I have no information that $100,000 was paid to architects.
It was pointed out the qtlier day that the payments amounted to $100,000.
That was the figure of the hon. member for East Simcoe, and I did not feel like taking the responsibility of the correctness of his figures.
Does the minister say that $100,000 was not paid out to architects?

I do. The hon. gentleman knows that included in the amount were moneys paid to the engineer in connection with the works at St. Andrew's rapids for engineering work, and also the amounts paid as prizes tor competitive plans.

The amount paid to the engineer was a very small proportion of the whole, and I fail to understand the distinction which the hon. gentleman draws with respect to the prizes, which were payments to architects for plans, whether competitive or otherwise. They were plans for a new building that was to be erected by the government, and it was felt that the chief architect was not equal to the job, and therefore prizes were offered to other architects. I think the sooner the minister remodels his architectural department the better it will be for the country. It is one of the most outrageous things the way that branch of tne Puolic Works Department is managed.
Montreal military buildings-new stores building, $10,000.

This is in tne same position as the item for the Montreal barracks. I am asking for a revote, and the purchase of the land will be made when the money is received from the city of Montreal. The contract has not been let, and will not be let until that arrangement is made.
Montreal new postal station S3- site and building, St. Catherine street, $20,000.
This is for the completion of postal station B.
What does that building cost, including the site?
Incluuing everything, the cost will be $126,036.25.
Is it expected that this will finish the building, and when will it be occupied?
I visited it on Sunday last.
When will it be completed ?

It is completed; the men are working in the office.
Montreal, new postal station, Pointe St. Charles, $21,875.
What will the site cost ?
It has not been purchased, we expect to close for the site shortly.
Have you no idea of the probable cost ?
This is a revote. There has been difficulty in getting a site and plans will not be prepared until the site is obtained.
What did Mr. Perrault receive on the buildings he constructed ?
5 per cent.
On the extras too ?
Yes.
What was It expected that this pneumatic system would cost ?
I think nearly half a million dollars ; we abandoned the scheme.
To what account is the loss on that pneumatic tube system, which a merchant would call dead stock, charged ?
When the money is paid out so much is charged and when the land and the pipes are sold that will be credited.
Are you using the motor cars that were in use some time ago ?
No, we are not using motor cars although we may later on. They can only be used in the summer.

In Toronto they were used all the year round.
Montreal, eastern postal station, $25,000.

This is to purchase a site in St. James division of Montreal for the erection of a public building for n branch post office in the eastern part of the city. There has been a request by the Postmaster General for this as being very much needed for postal accommodation. This will be station ' C '.
What will it cost ?
Mi\ PUGSLEY. It is in the same position as the other, no plans have been prepared.
Will it be better or worse than iSt. Charles ?

Of course the people of the eastern portion of Montreal claim that they are as much entitled to a line postal station as those of the west. My hon. friend (Mr. Ames) knows how important Ste. Catherine Street has become ; it is now so to speak the boulevard of Montreal. From a postal point of view, we thought we should divide Montreal into three stations, the central post office, section ' B ' in the west and section ' C ' in the east. That other station at St. Charles will serve some of the suburbs that have been annexed or will be shortly.
Does this come next to the Iloclielaga district ?
I think the new postal station ' C ' will be built on the confines of St. James and St. Maurice divisions. It will be quite a distance from Hoenelaga.
What class of pipe is it that is stored on this lot which you purchased for the purpose ?
We did not purchase a lot for it, it is the ordinary cast iron pipe, 10 inches in size.

The minister will agree that pipe deteriorates in value every day unless it is under thoroughly good cover and there must be a sufficiently good demand in Canada for pipe of that size for the government to dispose of it.
We have been endeavouring to sell it and have received certain offers which we have not thought satisfactory. We are holding for a somewhat higher price.
How much did the lot cost on which this shed is put ?
It was bought some years ago, and I have not the figures in hand.

What did the shed
cost ?
A very small sum. We had the material on the lot and used that material. The cost was trifling.

The lot was not purchased for the purpose of storing the pipes. We purchased the lot near the Bonaventure station in order to have a station of our own near the railway. Before the new annex to the general post office was built, the newspaper part of the post office business took up too much space in the building. The bags containing the newspapers were sent to the central office, and there was al-

ways heaps of bags blocking the street and Fortification lane. We decided to have a special place of our own near Bonaventure station for our newspaper business. The different newspapers, the ' Star,' the ' Gazette,' ' La Patrie ' and others would send their bags to the station and they would be taken by the railways just across the street.
Does the hon. minister say that this lot on Imperial avenue is to be used as the location of a station 7

No. The lot near Bonaventure station was got for that purpose. When we got the addition to the post office, that station was np more needed. So, we were left with the original lot on our hands. The Grand Trunk wanted the lot for some railway purpose and we exchanged the lot for the present one which is used for the storage of pipe. I do not pretend to know the conditions of the exchange.

That is exactly the point I am trying to bring out. If we found the lot opposite Bonaventure station could not be used for the purpose originally intended, and the Grand Trunk wanted it, why did not the government sell the lot to the Grand Trunk for what they paid for it? Why did they exchange and get a lot on the side street, and now decide that they have no use for it and simply hold it ?
My hon. friend knows that if we get in exchange a value similar to that we should get in a sale, it is equivalent to a sale. The government has lost nothing.
Would the hon. minister (Mr. Lemieux) rather have a real estate in Montreal or money in the treasury ? Which is the more liquid asset of the two ?
With the boom there is in real estate in Montreal, land there is as good as hard cash.
I think the hon. minister will find it rather hard to dispose of the Imperial avenue property on the basis of value equal to that of the lot opposite Bonaventure station.

I am afraid the hon. member for St. Antoine (Mr. Ames) does not understand the business methods of this government. In this case, they have simply done what they have always done. They always do the -wrong thing; never by any chance or accident do they do the right thing, the thing that any business man -would do. The Grand Trunk wanted this lot opposite Bonaventure station

naturally they wanted it to enlarge their premises. Having a lot in an undesirable portion of the city from a business standpoint, and. desiring to get rid of it, they went to the government which is an easy mark-for its friends-and proposed an exchange, and, of course, the government got the worst of
it. Probably the land they gave to the Grand Trunk was worth anywhere from three to five times that which the Grand Trunk gave to the government. That is the only way for this government to do business ; it is the way they have always done it. Instead of selling the lot as a business man would have done, they exchanged it for the property on a side street, which, I fancy, will be on their hands as long as they want a place to store pipes.
What is the approximate value of the pipe held in Montreal by the department ? Also, what did the government pay for the 10-inch pipe ?

I shall be glad to obtain that information for my hon. friend. He can understand that we are not dealing tonight with 'the question of the pneumatic system, a matter which was disposed of some time ago.
So long as the minister will bring dow7n the information I am satisfied.
I will get a complete statement of the cost and of the present situation.
And I would advise the government to dispose of that pipe for thel best price they can get. The sooner they get out of it the better.
I agree that we should dispose of it, but at a fair price.

On page Y-43 of the Auditor General's Report, I find an item in connection with the postal station on St. Catherine street :
Thomas Parent, clerk of works, 274 days at $3, $822.
Wrhat special qualification had this gentleman for this office ?
He was employed in 1900. I have no definite information on this point to-night, but I am told that he was an experienced builder.
Perhaps the minister could tell me what official in his department made the negotiations for the exchange with the Grand Trunk of these two lots that have been referred to.
I cannot give that at once, because it was done quite a while ago and before I came into parliament.
Will the minister bring down that information ?
I shall be glad to do so.

To verify the statement I made some time ago to the Postmaster General that in the smaller offices he does not give any rent allow-ance,* I would refer him to appendix D of his report. He will find there such offices as Havelock, Hawk

Lake, Hawley, Hawthorne, and so on, and in none of these is there any rent allowance.
It is included in the salary.
But the salary in these cases is $18.75. How much would the hon. gentleman allow for rent ?
There is more than that for salary, surely.
Then, the hon. gentleman's report is no use.
These post offices may have been opened after part of the year had passed.
The report gives forwarding allowance, salary based on the revenue of the previous year, $18.75, in a number of these cases.

That is for part of the year only. These post offices may have been opened late in the year. In the salary are included the rent allowance and the fuel allowance.
Montreal-new examining warehouse, $405,000.

This is to make provision for the balance due on the purchase price, which was $402,000. An agreement for the purchase of this property was arrived at some time ago for the sum of $402,000, but the payment is not to be made until the 1st of May. We expect probably that the time will be extended to 15th July. We agreed to pay $10,000 in cash, and the balance with 5 per cent interest. This amount will make 5 per cent interest up to 15th July next. The property was purchased upon the urgent representation of the collector of customs, Mr. White, at the port of Montreal, and Mr. McDougall, the Commissioner of Customs. Their opinion was that this was an ideal site for the customs building, and an opportunity arose to acquire the property. It consists of 07,800 square feet. It has a frontage of 495 feet on the north side of McGill street, and is substantially a lot of 400 feet by 140. There are a number of old buildings on it. The property is the old Grey Nunnery property, and is situated nearly opposite the new Grand Trunk offices. Mr. White's opinion was that the opportunity to purchase this land ought not to be allowed to pass. The question was forced to the front by reason of the lire which occurred when the examining warehouse was injured. It is supposed that this will be used for a custom house as well as an examining warehouse. We have not decided when we shall start to build.
$10,000. you say, was paid to secure the lot. Has the government become bankrupt that it had to pay in instalments?
This $10,000 was required to be paid by Governor General's warrant, and the collector of customs secured the lot by making this payment on the option.
Is the property revenue producing at the present time?
There are eight tenants on the property, paying a rental of about $4,800.	[DOT]

Can the minister give us an assurance that the work of erection will be undertaken at an early day? Since the fire in the Montreal custom house this work has become imperative, and we would be glad to know that the plans will be made and the wo-k commenced soon.

I cannot give any assurance to-night. We are spending a good deal of money in the city of Montreal, and having acquired the land at a large expense, we think we have done pretty well. I am not able to say when the new building will be commenced.
When the government determine to build, will an opportunity be afforded to architects to submit plans?
I cannot say.

I thought all these plans for public buildings were prepared in the depai'tment. We would like to have an assurance that in this case they will be prepared in the department.
Mr. FIELDING, One hon. gentleman wants competitive plans, and another wants them made at Ottawa.

I cannot give an assurance to both.
Mr. FOWLER, In the interest of the country I would like to have that assurance from the minister to-night. Will this expensive staff of his prepare these plans?
I may say to the hon. gentleman that the practice of the department is to prepare the plans in the department, and I have no reason to supnose that that practice will be departed from in this case.
The practice is quite otherwise.
With some few exceptions.
That proves the rule.

It is delightful to have the minister with a wave of his hand say ' with some trifling exceptions,' when we are paying out $100,000 for architectural assistance. I hope the Minister of Public Works will insist that the Architectural Department shall be something more than an Architectural Department in name only and that it shall actually do some work for the

country. It seems to be more ornamental than useful.

I have totalled up the expenditure which it is contemplated to undertake in connection with new post office facilities in Montreal, including the addition to the post office, station B, station 0 and the Point St. Charles station, and it makes altogether $1,126,272. Adding to that the new examining warehouse site, which has cost $405,000, you have a total of $1,531,272.
Montreal has got to be a very important city. Last year the revenue from customs duties was $11,433,595, and from excise $4,496,431. The exports were $70,000,000 and the imports $73,000,000.
Does the minister mean by that that the city of Montreal did all this? How much of it was contributed by the country around ?
Do you desire to vote against this item?
I think it is a poor piece of business to spend over $400,000 to buy a site you do not propose to use.
I did not say that.
You said that you did not propose to use it now.
I said I could not give any assurance when the work would begin.
You are not proposing to use it or you could give that assurance. You are renting it for $400 a year which does not represent one per cent upon the value. The taxation upon it will be heavy.
There does not happen to be any taxation.
Well, that is very fortunate. If there were it would absorb the whole amount of your revenue.

I would like to ask the government for some information in regard to the amount of $25,000 which was paid in connection with this new pneumatic tube system. An architect was employed to prepare plans for the building that it was intended to erect, and the government have paid that architect more than $7,000 for the preparation of plans that were of no value to the government or anybody else. The government have purchased tubes and have paid large amounts of money for them.
How do you know they were purchased in the United States?
I think that Sir Wm. Mu-loclc said in the House they were purchased in the United States or in the old country.
My information is that they were purchased in Glasgow.

Well, they were not made in Canada anyway. The department, after proposing to adopt a pneumatic tube system and after paying out a large amount of money, abandoned the whole scheme both in Montreal and Toronto. One would have supposed that when a new system was being adopted it would have been sufficient to have experimented with it in one city rather than in two.
But the old rivalry.
The hon. Postmaster General has stated that the' total expenditure in connection with this pneumatic tube system if completed would have been nearly half a million dollars.
I am going to bring down a statement in regard to the pneumatic tube system showing what it cost and the quantity and value of the property on hand.

I would like my hon. friend to produce before the committee at some future date a statement of the total expenditure of money for every purpose by this government in connection with the adoption of the pneumatic tube system in Toronto and Montreal.
That is what I promised to do.
At the same time showing what the government have on hand for the expenditure and what they propose to do with these tubes.
I see by the Auditor General's Report, V-43, ' F. St. Germain, commission on valuation of property, $116.' I would like to inquire what property that was.
I presume that would be the lot of land that was purchased.
The Bona venture station lot?
Yes.
What would be the value of that property?

In the vicinity of $25,-
000.
Who did the buying of this $405,000 property?
Mr. Wright.
What pay did he get?
He was employed by the collector, not by my department.
Did the collector of customs in Montreal, on his own initiative without the instruction of the department buy this land ?

The collector of customs being of opinion it was urgent this

lot should be bought, communicated with the commissioner of customs and the commissioner of customs authorized him to get an option upon the property and he employed Mr. Wright to do so. My information is that there was no arrangement as to what commission Mr. Wright should get or as to -whether he should get any commission. Mr. Wright has made a claim for commission which I have not recognized as yet.
How much ?
I think it is in the vicinity of $2,000.
It is strange the collector of customs should take an option upon this lot on his own responsibility and pay $10,000 on the option.
Not on his own responsibility. After he had made the preliminary arrangement the commissioner of customs came to me and requested me to approve of the option and I did.
And this $10,000 was paid by Mr. White, collector of customs, out of his own privy purse ?
It was paid by him, but I do not know out of what purse he paid it.
Was it paid by the minister ?
A few days afterwards it was.
Never mind the number of days ; did Mr. White, collector of customs, pay this $10,000 out of his own pocket ?
I do not know that. I believe he paid it.

To the best of my recollection, Mr. White was authorized and he authorized a special agent. The object was not to let it be known who was to buy the property, because the moment it was known that the government was purchasing, the government would have gone up. Mr. White rendered service in that way and it was quite creditable on his part.

I have not as yet condemned the transaction, because I do not know what it is. It is laudable curiosity on my part, because it seems strange that a private individual should pay $10,000 to secure an option for the government. Did the collector provide the money himself.

All I know is that when the commissioner of customs told me that Mr. White desired to purchase the property, I told him I could not supply the money because there was no Governor General's warrant. The arrangement was authorized Mr. PUGSLEY.
however, and Mr. Wright secured the option and a few days afterwards the Governor General's warrant was made out and the money transmitted to the Customs Department.
Was there need for great haste ?
There was.
Was the property in the market ?
Yes, and others were after it.
The property had been offered for sale ?

I believe not.
Nicolet public building, $10,000.

This Nicolet building has been in course of construction for the last two years. In 1907 $204 and in 1908 $136 or in all $340 was spent in advertising for tenders which is 2i per cent of the total cost, or as much as the architect's fees.

It is hard to please hon. gentlemen opposite ; if we don't advertise we are criticised, and if we do advertise we are criticised.
Mr. FOWLER, building cost ?

over $20,000.
Mr. IfOWLER. works ?

Mr. FOWLER, occupation ?
How much has the The total cost is a little Who is the clerk of Mr. Rivet.
What was his previous
He was a practical builder, I understand.
Do you find that in your notes or are you making it up.
You should not suggest anything of that kind.
How many days did he work there ?
I cannot say.
How long did his job last ?
The contract was let on June 26, 1906, and it was to be completed October 30, 1907.
It is quite a graft this inspector business.

Don't say anything
nasty at this early hour of the morning.
That is not nasty.
When you mention graft it is very annoying.

I quite understand it is
to the hon. gentleman. What do you pay this inspector a day ?
Three dollars.

I want to direct the attention of the minister to the precaution Mr. Hyman took when he appointed these inspectors. Mr. Hyman wrote a letter to those who nominated the inspectors which will be found in ' Hansard ' 1906, page 6730 :
In recommendations for inspectors, foremen or clerks of works, to have charge of the construction or authorized to oversee and inspect the erection or repairing of public works, it is imperative that the party recommended have a practical experience and be capable of thoroughly understanding plans and specifications and of seeing that they are properly and correctly carried out. Attention to this matter will obviate delays which have taken place through men being recommended who, on inquiry, were found not to be qualified for the work and. therefore, could not be employed.
The hon. minister at that time said :
A copy of that letter is sent in every case when recommendations are made.
Hoes the hon. minister carry out the policy laid down by Mr. Hyman ?
Yes.
Will the hon. minister lay on the table the letter addressed to this gentleman and his reply at the next meeting of the committee ?
All I can do Is to give the hon. gentleman the form, which is a printed form on which the blanks are filled in.

Not only is this a printed form, but it is a mere form. It has no practical effect, and is not intended to have any practical effect. The only object of having this form of letter is to bring it down to this committee when the matter is under discussion. It is sent out or course, but the man who receives it pays no attention to it, and probably throws it into the waste-paper basket, fine hon. member for Peel must know that.
In making calculations for public buildings for the coming year, does the hon. minister calculate on the same length of working day as hitherto ?
I know of no difference.
Then, am I to understand that the Bill introduced by Mr. Verville for an eight-hour day will not be allowed by the government to pass?
That would be a farfetched conclusion.
The minister has just stated that the length of the working day would be the same as hitherto.
Is the hon. gentleman in favour of an eight-hour day?

It is quite evident that the government is not in favour of it.
Plessisyille-public building, $2,000.
This is a revote. There was an appropriation of $3,000 last year, of which $2,800 was paid for the site.
What is the size of the village?
Its population in 1901 Was 1,300.

How large is the site ?
Mr. PUtxSLEY. It is a corner lot, 50 feet by 100 feet.

From whom was it
bought?
From Mr. Beausoleil.
What is the total cost ?
The plans are not yet prepared, but it is supposed that it will be about $25,000.

What is the postal
revenue?

It was $1,327.30 for the nine months.
Quebec citadel-drill shed for school of gunnery, $10,000.

This is a revote. This drill shed has been urged by the Minister of Militia and Defence since June, .1905. He regards it as most important that the service should be provided with it. The minister states that there will be accommodation for at least one of every type of gun used in Canada for instructional purposes. He also says that in winter instruction cannot be given for artillery work unless all guns for instructional purposes are kept in premises which are heated. The minister has urged this very strongly, and it is proposed to proceed this year with the building.
What is the total cost ?
As the Minister of Militia should be here to explain this item, I think that it had better stand.
We had better finish Quebec.

There, should not be so much delay at the beginning of the session. From November 22 to December 17 we did not earn enough to feed a cat and here we

are sitting at 1.30 in the morning and the minister is not satisfied with that.
Quebec .citadel-Governor Generali quari ters, repairs, furniture, &c., $2,000.
This is to make provision for some renewals, repairs, &e., to the Governor General's quarters in the citadel. The chief item is painting, $1,020.
At whose request are they made ?
A request is made to the Public Works Department by the controller for His Excellency stating what repairs and improvements are needed.
Is this on account of the festivities.

NO, some further expenditures will be required which will be provided for in the supplementaries.
Quebec drill hall-addition to building and levelling ground $9,000.

This is to raise the roof of the armouries and to extend the drill hall on some land which has been expropriated to afford much needed accommodation to the new corps to be formed, the present accommodation being entirely insufficient.
We want information about this. Some people think that we have a sufficient number of these corps in the country. Is this cavalry, infantry or artillery ?
I cannot give the information.
I am sure it is infantry.

We are dealing with so many armouries to-night that the Minister of Militia should be present to give information about them. We receive only partial information, valuable information is not furnished ; we are going it blind.
Who was the owner of the land expropriated ?
' The name is not given in my note. The property is situated on Grande Alice.
Perhaps the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Morin) could supply the name ?
I know the man's name very well. That is why I ask you. He made a good many thousand dollars in a few weeks. And he is not the member for Dorchester, you can bet on that.
If there are middlemen in this transaction, I think that should be explained.
There are no middlemen.
What was the cost of the land ?
It was $20,220.64. The land expropriated was 9,240 square feet. There are to be two additions to the building, one on each end.
Did you buy land on both ends ?
I think not.
Can the minister give us the name of the man who expropriated the land ?
Three valuators were placed upon the property, but whether in connection with the expropriation or not I am not aware. They were Alex. Gauvreau, F. Turcott, and L. P. Sirois.
Three Tories. The man who owned the property, to blindfold the government, got three Tories to put a value on it, so as to hide the thing a little bit.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: These Tories are always getting us into trouble.
It was a trick. He knew that if Grits did the trick they would be blamed, so he got three Tories to do that kind of work.
How much were they paid?
This was four years ago, and I have not the figures at hand.
This was bought in 1904. At what time in 1904 ?

December 6.
Ml-. FOWLER. Oh, that was carrying out a pre-election pledge.
How was that ?
It was done just after election.

That man did not need an election ; he is in the Senate.
Quebec examining warehouse-alterations, fittings, &c., $1,500.
This is to put in an electric lighting system in the examining warehouse, as requested by the Customs Department in 1907.
What does it cost to make the change ?

Quebec immigrant buildings-additions, renewals, repairs, &c., $7,500.
Mr. PUGSLEY'. This is for work to be undertaken during the fiscal year.
Is this let by contract ?

No, it is a number of small amounts and done by day's work.

Quebec immigrant hospital for trachoma and kindred diseases in Savard park-reconstruction of building destroyed by fire, $5,000.
The total cost of this work is $90,000.
This is for the immigrants brought in by the government. The $5-a-head immigrants, I suppose. Is the contract let ?
Yes, the building is finished.
Who had the contract ?
Messrs. Jinchereau & Lamonde for $05,000.
How do you get it up to $90,000 ?

There were a number of items. That made the total expenditure up to November 30, of $71,750. Then there is an amount due on contract, $7,018; wiring, $777: call bells, $285; sidewalks, fencing and water service, $1,400; furniture. $1,000; contingencies and superintendence. $3,030.
I thought these people suffering from trachoma were sent back to the country from which they came.
They cannot be sent back immediately, and even when they are deported, we have to treat them like human beings while they are awaiting deportation.
Who was the clerk of works at the hospital?
Mr. E. M. Talbot, the architect, was the clerk of works.

The Auditor General's Report differs from the statement of the minister. I find that not only was there an architect, Mr. Talbot, who got a commission of $911, but there "was a clerk of works. Leo Yermette, and other clerk of works, D. J. Mullarkey.
Mr. Mullarkey was sent from the head office here.

We were told yesterday by the minister that this work was well inspected because Mr. Mullarkey was sent down as clerk of works. Now we have in this case an architect and we have two clerks of works. Mr. Mullarkey is paid $4 per day. So, the minister is badly informed. This only gives a partial account of the services of the clerk of works. The service is from July 1 to December 27. Let us see what further services were rendered by Mr. Vermette. Was there any further service?

Not in my memorandum. You may have it in the Auditor General's Report. We have a resident
agent at Quebec and I suppose he was employed by him.
Then who is Talbot ?
An architect.
Did he draw the plans ?
No.
What did he do ?
He superintended the construction of the work.
What did Mr. Yermette do ?
He was engaged at $2 per day. I presume he was under Mr. Talbot.
And what did Mr. Mullarkey do ?
Mr. Mullarkey would be sent to make an inspection.
But it was all inspected.
