Mr. Vermette appears to have been paid $2 per day. Mr. Mullarkey is employed in the department and he is an expert in concrete work although well qualified to inspect all buildings. He is sent out here and there by the chief architect to inspect work which is in progress of construction and that is the way he did in this particular case. I understood that when we were discussing some other items the department were commended for having an expert of this character to inspect works from time to time.

No, that is not what was referred to at the time when that was spoken of ; it was another matter altogether. It was not in connection with Mr. Mullarkey. The minister stated that before these progress estimates were paid a gentleman went down from the department to inspect as to the progress estimates and that was commended as being a proper thing to do. Here we have an architect employed in connection with this work. Did Talbot draw the plans ?
Mr. PUGSLEY'. They were drawn in the department.
All he did was to inspect ?
Yes.

Would the minister bring down information as to how much was paid to Mr. Talbot, Mr. Vermette and Mr. Mullarkey in connection with this detention hospital ?
Quebec military buildings-main store building at Dominion arsenal, $21,000.

This is an item in regard to which there is a wonderful lack of information. The minister who is supposed to

give us information on military matters lias not been here to-night, and it is unfortunate that when an item of $20,000 or $30,000 is called we cannot get the information which we require.

This item is to make provision for the construction of a main stores building at the Dominion arsenal. The land was purchased on the 6th of October, 4906. It is situated at the corner of Carle-ton and Arsenal streets.
Will the hon. gentleman give us a list of the papers in which the advertisement was inserted ?
I could not this evening but I would be glad to do so if the hon. gentleman thinks it important.
What is the policy of the department in that regard ? Is all the advertising given to his political friends or is the advertisement inserted in the principal papers in the district ?
Who was it purchased from and at what cost ?
From A. Grenier at a cost of $3,000. The building will be three storeys, built on stone and cement foundations with a frontage of 91 feet on Carle-ton street and 53 feet on Arsenal street.
cost ?

at Ottawa.

of the contract ?

The general rule is that we select a number of the leading newspapers in the district where the works are to be advertised. I think I am safe in saying that the newspapers selected are friendly to the government.
iMr. BLAIN. In every case ?
Not in every case, but in the great majority of cases. We are careful to see they are newspapers of large circulation, so as to give full publicity to the advertisement.
Then I am to understand that in no case is an advertisement inserted in a Conservative newspaper?
If the hon. gentleman desires. I will be very glad to bring down a list of the newspapers in which this advertisement was inserted.
What is the policy of the uepartment in this respect?
The policy of the department is to advertise as widely as is thought necessary to give full publicity to the call for tenders.
If a work is being done in a town where the Conservative newspaper has the largest and widest circulation, is the advertisement inserted in that newspaper?

Such a case has not yet been brought to my notice in the short time I have been minister as a Tory newspaper having tue largest circulation, but if such an unusual thing should occur I would consider the matter.
In my own town the Conservative newspaper has the largest circulation.
And the total cost ?
$50,587.82, but that includes the cost of the site, heating, electric wiring, fixtures, sidewalks, fences and elevator.
There is an item of $332 for advertising. Will the minister explain that ?
That would be advertising for tenders in the various newspapers.
What is the name of your town?

I do not propose to take these flippant jokes from the minister. It is all very well for him to joke over these large expenditures, but it is a serious matter. The Conservative paper has the largest circulation in my own town, it is so in the adjoining county and it is so in South Simcoe.
Two or three of them.

I could name them by the hundreds in the province of Ontario.
Mr. SPROULE, You may mention Owen Sound, Meaford and Collingwood.
The hon. minister has not been very much in Ontario.
No. I hope to be more.

I hope so, and I hope the minister will treat these expenditures more seriously. Then we are to understand that the policy of the department is that these advertisements are not to be inserted in Conservative newspapers.
Mr. CAltVELL. Cut it short.
The hon. gentleman was cut short in the elections in his province the oilier day.
That is ancient history.

It is not, as the hon. gentleman will find when he goes back for election. Is it the policy of the Minister of Public Works to advertise for tenders in the largest newspapers regardless of their policy ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That has always been the policy in the past ?
It has not been the policy of this government in the past.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Or the other governments.
Is it the policy of the Ontario government ?
The hon. gentleman was a member of the Ontario government, and he ought to know.
I am speaking of the Whitney government.
Would I offend the hon. gentleman (Mr. Blain) if I asked him whether he was in favour of this item or not ?
The Minister of Public Works might try by asking me the question. I hope he will not deal with these questions in such a flippant manner.
I was curious to know if the hon. gentleman objected to the item.
I want to know if any of this $500 was paid to any Liberal-Conservative newspaper.
Not very likely.
If that is for a public work in Quebec, I can say that it was advertised in the Quebec * Morning Chronicle.'

We will have to see aoout that.
23G
I hope it won't occur again.
I want the hon. gentleman to bring down a list of the newspapers in which this was advertised.
I shall be pleased to.
And I shall also ask him to announce the policy of the department in this matter at a future sitting.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I hope my hon. friend (Mr. Blain) will, in the meantime, look into the policy of some few years ago, because it would strengthen his case very much if he could show that under the Conservative government any Liberal newspaper got an advertisement.

Whenever wrong-doing by this government is pointed out, the Finance Minister flies to a comparison with the old administration. He thinks it is right to advertise in party newspapers alone because the Liberal-Conservative government did it in days gone by. Surely that is not a sufficient answer. What I say is that where there is a Conservative newspaper which has the largest circulation in a town where work is going on, the department should advertise in that [DOT] newspaper.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend really must not expect us to be too good. We are rising to great heights of virtue, but I am afraid we cannot get as much superior to the former government as the hon. gentleman wishes us to be.

The hon. minister seems to think that there are no towns where Conservative papers have a larger circulation than Liberal papers. I could point to towns in the province from which he comes where that is the case. The Conservative newspapers in New Brunswick enjoy by far the largest circulation among the mass of newspapers in that province. Why was it found necessary to pay $332 for advertising for these military buildings when the advertising for the immigration building cost only $85 ?
I cannot tell that. There may have been a wider circulation given.
Were the advertisements confined to the Quebec papers?

No. They would take in the Montreal dailies, and possibly the Ottawa dailies, besides the weekly papers in the district.
Quebec east public building, $30,000.
What is this for?
The post office at St. Roch's.
What did you pay for the site?
What is the total cost of the building?
It has not been erected yet.
How was the land purchased?
By arbitration.
From whom was it bought?
From three different owners. As it was done very recently, I have not the names here.
Who were the arbitrators ?
Mr. McCarthy, the engineer at Quebec, was the one acting for the government.
What is the building expected to cost when completed?
What was the price the owners asked for the land?

I do not know what the owner asked, but he is dissatisfied -with the award.
Sherbrooke drill hall, $20,000.
This is for a drill hall at Sherbrooke on a site which has been already acquired. The contract has been let for the sum of $82,500.

We have passed four or five items for militia buildings, and I think the Minister of Militia should be here to explain them. The Minister of Railways told me yesterday he did not think there would be enough money to put up a new station at Truro. I protest against these expenditures when there are other places where buildings are more urgently needed.
The building is to be of brick with stone lintels, resting on a stone basement. The frontage is 157 feet on Bellevidere avenue.
When will this be completed ?

The contract is to be completed by November 7, 1909.
St. Henri post office-improvements, $1,200.
This is to provide for a fire-escape ladder and the construction of a granolithic sidewalk and also a basement.
Does the government pay the whole cost of the sidewalk ?
Yes.
The minister said the other day that the rule was to pay only one-half.

I do not think the rule can be uniform ; in some cases the town Mr. PUGSLEY.
has the local improvement system and then they assess the owners of the property. The government, although not legally bound to do so, usually pays its share. The usual course is for the government to pay the whole cost of granolithic sidewalks around its own buildings.
St. Hyacinthe public building-improvement, repairs, &c., $2,500.
This is to provide for a number of repairs and improvements, including a fire escape.
Some friend of the government must be making fire escapes and selling them for these various public buildings.

I understand that since that very deplorable accident in Montreal in which a number of lives were lost, a municipal by-law has been passed requiring fire escapes to be placed on all public buildings.
St. John's military buildings-stables for cavalry, $25,000.

This is to make provision towards the erection of stables for cavalry at the military buildings there. The work is under way, the contract has been let and the total probable cost is $37,188. The stables will accommodate some 85 horses.
How many cavalry are there at present.
About 75.

I think we should have an understanding that, when we are dealing with so many buildings for the Militia Department, we shall expect the Minister of Militia to be here to give us information as to the needs which are said to justify these expenditures.
The hon. gentleman got every information.

The hon. minister gave us no information on that point. He simply told us that this building was to accommodate 85 horses. He has not told us anything of the strength of the force at this place or anything to show why the building is needed. Somebody must have asked for the building and 'must have asked for it on some data.
I gave the number of horses and men.
In a number of cases, my hon. friend (Mr. Fowler) has asked questions, but got no information.
I told the hon. gentleman this was for 85 horses and that the force there consisted of 75 men.

That was in this case, but in others in which the hon. gentleman

(Mr. Fowler) inquired, he got no information. We should have this information from the Militia Department. I do not know whether the minister (Mr. Pugsley) is sincere, or whether he is depending on jollying the House along. I think we should be treated more seriously, and I think we are entitled to all the information.
What information would the kon, gentleman like with regard to this building ?
I am speaking of these items generally.
But take this item.

I will take what items I like. On this page that we have been going over, we have a vote for a quarantine station, and about that we got a little information. There is a vote for an immigration building, and we got'very little information about that-the minister could hardly be expected to give it. There was a vote for the Montreal barracks, nut no one representing the Militia Department gave us information about that. The Militia Department is spending very large sums of money and the country is beginning to get a little restless, regarding this expenditure as extravagant. On the vote for Montreal post office we got practically no information. Here was a vote for another militia building in Montreal and we got practically no information in regard to that. Then we took up the Quebec drill hall and got no information about that, then another military building in Quebec, about which we learned very little. There was a vote for the drill hall at Sherbrooke, and we were referred to the honourable member for the riuing tiur. "Worthington), who happens not to be in his place and who, in any event, is not charged with responsibility of giving information to the House.
Mr. PUGSLEY'. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) says he gets very little information about these votes, but will he tell us what information he wants with regard to this vote.

I say that with regard to all these we are entitled to information from the Minister of Militia as well as from the Minister of Public Works, because the demand for these buildings comes from the Militia Department.
Mi-. PUGSLEY. If the hon. gentleman will tell me what information he wants
I am talking about all these votes, and I am not going to be put off in that flippant way by the Minister of Public Works, and I want him to understand that.

You don't want the information; you want an excuse for talking against it.
236J

I am not talking against time or trying to kill time. The way the minister has acted for the last two or three hours would indicate that he is not sincerely endeavouring to do the duties devolving upon a minister in this House, and I think I have the right to speak about it. When we are voting $6,000,000 or $7,000,000 to be expended for militia purposes every year, we are entitled to know what the money is to be spent for. When it is proposed to spend $80,000 or $90,000 for the militia building, as in these cases, we want to know why the building is needed and how it is to be used. It may be said that the Minister of Public Works cannot be expected to give this information, I admit that. But for that very reason, the Minister of Militia should be here to give us the information we require. If a vote relating to the post office comes up, the Postmaster General (Mr. Lemieux) is here to give us information. And, when we are voting money to put up these expensive buildings for the Militia Department, I think we shall expect and demand that the Minister of Militia be here to give us information.
Does the hon. gentleman want information about this building at St. Johns ?
How many men and horses compose the force there ?
There are seventy-five men and eighty-five horses.
How much is this building going to cost ?
The estimate is $37,188.79.
The country should know that for eighty-five horses and seventy-five men it is going to cost about $40,000.
This is only for the horses, not for the men.

Then, the information given is not correct.
Mr. PUGSLEY'. In what respect ? This building is for stables for the cavalry. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) asks how many horses are kept and how many men are in the force, and I tell him eighty-five horses and seventy-five men.
, How 'long have the cavalry been stationed at St. John ?
About three years.

Translation.) Mr. Chairman, I may say in connection with the item under discussion, that is the erection of stables for cavalry at the military school of St. John, that this school has 75 men in training, which involves the

use of 85 horses. These stables were built for the reason that the Militia Department has none at ail there.
There was formerly at St. John a school of infantry, but some three years ago the department decided to establish a school of cavalry at that place, and of course stables had to be provided. These are beautiful stables. I am astonished that only about $35,000 all told, will have been spent by the government on that contract. St. John's military school is an old institution dating as far back as 1876, and I believe these stables were absolutely necessary to maintain its efficiency.

I want to say something respecting the necessity of the Minister of Militia being here when these estimates are going through. We have in this list of Quebec buildings seven that belong to the Militia Department, and the Minister of Militia is not here to give us any information with respect to the necessity of these buildings. The Minister of Public Works cannot give us the information. He draws largely on his imagination, he looks at the paper and says the first thing that comes into his mind.
What does the hon. member want to know about this item?

I want to know what necessity exists for this building that requires such a great expense. I think that the present stables at St. John's are quite sufficient for these horses without spending nearly $20,000 for new stables.
What is the total number of troops at this station.
About seventy-five.
What accommodation has been provided for these horses since the corps has been established at St. John's ?
There was an old drill shed which was converted into a temporary stable for the horses, pending the erection of new stables.
Have you a clerk of works there ?
Evariste Gagne is clerk of works, a carpenter?
He is paid on the basis of $3 per day, and is employed for about nine months.
Where are the stables located ?
On the east side of the Grand Trunk Railway.
Are they located inside of the old breastworks that were blown up about a century ago, or are they between the barracks and the river ?
On the ground of the fort.
Of these military grounds?
Yes.
The government own the site ?
Yes.
How many acres of military grounds have you there?

12 x 8 acres.
St. John's public buildings, $10,000.

This is a revote. It is for the purpose of continuing work in connection with the erection of a new public building for post office purposes and, I presume, for customs purposes as well. It is a building 03 x* 44 feet, two storeys, basement and mansard.
What is the cost?
The total estimated cost, including everything, is $43,910.
